# PREFACE.

What is presented here to you, Christian Reader, is a *True and Faithful Relation, and so forth <note>original: "&c."</note>* (as the title states, and as will be further clarified by this Preface). Although because of its handling <note>original: "carriage"</note> in some respects, and by its very nature as well, it might be judged and called a *Work of Darkness*, it was actually offered with great tenderness and caution to the highest-ranking men in Europe—kings and princes. Except for those in England, everyone listened to it with great respect for a time. Some gladly embraced and hosted it for a long while; the reputation <note>original: "Fame"</note> of it reached Rome, causing the Pope to take action, as he did not know what the outcome might be or how much it might affect him.

Indeed, it filled all people, both the learned and the unlearned in most places, with great wonder and astonishment. All of these things will be shown and proven (to the fullest extent of what I have said) in the contents of this book through unquestionable records and evidence. Therefore, I have no doubt that many people will be found in the world whose curiosity will lead them to read *what I think is unparalleled in its kind by any book that has been published in any age*. I say this even if they read it for no other reason than to satisfy their curiosity.

However, whatever other men may seek for themselves in the reading of it, according to their various inclinations, I must sincerely profess here that the goal I propose for myself (insofar as I have contributed to publishing the work) is not to satisfy curiosity, but to do good and promote religion. When we were first acquainted with the book and were offered the chance to read it, we had recently been occupied with a very similar subject: *Mistaken Inspiration* and *Possession* caused by an ignorance of *natural causes*. <note>The author is referring to a previous work arguing that many "supernatural" claims were actually medical or psychological in origin.</note> As our aim in publishing that previous labor was to do good, we have had good reason since then to believe that we did not altogether miss our mark.

Because of this, we could not help but gladly accept this book. Just as we gladly accepted it, we read it to the end with equal eagerness and enthusiasm. When we had finished, it was truly our opinion that publishing it would be very timely and useful. It serves as a tool against atheists at all times, but especially in these times, when the spirit of error and illusion is so prevalent. This is seen not only in professed Anabaptists <note>A radical religious sect often associated with social disorder and claims of direct revelation in the 17th century.</note> of the worst kind that former ages have known and hated, but also in many others who openly (and, I hope, mostly heartily) reject the results such causes have produced in others. Nevertheless, these people still base their beliefs on the same principles of *supposed inspiration* and *imaginary revelations*, and on that account consider themselves to be much better Christians than others, if not the *only* true Christians. I was much confirmed in this judgment when I was told (by those who knew very well) that the most reverend, pious, and learned *Archbishop of Armagh* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), a highly respected scholar famous for his biblical chronology.</note>, lately

<summary>The author introduces a "True and Faithful Relation" concerning spiritual matters that once fascinated European royalty and alarmed the Pope. He argues that publishing these records will combat atheism and the "imaginary revelations" of religious radicals by demonstrating the reality of spiritual delusions.</summary>

...deceased, upon reading the mentioned book before his death, had expressed the same intention and wished it to be printed. But because it is very possible that not every reader will initially be able on their own to make good use of this serious story through logical inferences and observations as intended, my primary aim in this preface is to help them. And since it is no less likely that this immoral age will produce many who, like the *Sadducees* of old (that is, *Jewish Epicureans*), believe in no *spirit*, *angel*, or *resurrection*; and who, being filled with prejudice when they hear of so many spirits as are mentioned here, and so many strange apparitions of various kinds, will not only reject it themselves but will be ready to laugh at anyone else who gives any credit to such things. Although I will not take it upon myself to convert through reason anyone who is committed to such an opinion because of a wicked life—that is, through unjust practices, luxurious and lewd behaviors, or open profanity under the guise of *wit* and *gallantry* and the like—because I think it is very just for God to leave such people to the error and blindness of their own judgments. Consequently, without a miracle, there can be little hope for them. Yet I hope that those who are rational men, sober in their lives and conduct <note>original: "Conversations"</note>—such as I have known myself; yes, men of excellent talents <note>original: "parts"</note> in other areas, men who are both willing to hear and able to consider—that such men, I say, may receive some satisfaction from what I shall say and propose for their candid consideration in this matter. If we were to argue the case using *Scripture*, the business would soon be settled; for there is no other controversial point among men that I know of that can receive a more ample, full, clear, and speedy determination than this business of *spirits*, *witches*, and *apparitions* could, if the Word of God were the judge. But I will assume that I am dealing with those who, though they do not altogether deny the Word of God, will nonetheless not easily admit anything they think is contrary to *reason*, or at least cannot be supported by *reason*. I shall therefore refrain from all scriptural proofs and testimonies in this specific case, and I ask the Christian reader (who might otherwise rightly take offense) to take note of the reason why I refrain.

But although I will not use any Scripture for proof, I hope I may be allowed to use some scriptural words by way of application, which may perhaps direct us to a good method for examining this business. The Apostle says in one place, φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ, ἐμωράνθησαν: (*professing themselves to be wise, they became fools*). I shall not inquire about whom or upon what occasion it was spoken; I draw no argument from it. I use it only because there is a show of great wisdom in this skeptical opinion; and yet, as I believe, there is as much error and falsehood in it (that is, *folly*, as the word is often used) as in any other false opinion that is less popular. I will structure my discourse around this point: first, to inquire into what makes this opinion so popular and plausible, especially among those who claim more than ordinary wisdom; and then, secondly, to reveal it (as best I can) in its true colors, so that its folly or falsehood may be discernible even to ordinary judgments.

First, then (regarding those who deny *spirits*, etc.), we say: the world is full of imposture. To know this, and to observe it in all trades, in all professions, and in all ranks and degrees of men, is to know the world, and that is to be wise. Though we call them *jugglers*, they actually deserve to be thought of as the most straightforward men in the world who show their tricks openly in the streets for money; for they profess what they are. The truest jugglers are those who perform their feats (and they for mo-

(many too, most of them) under the veil and reputation of holiness, sanctity (or saintship), religion, virtue, justice, and friendship—fine words to catch men who are easily convinced and think that everything that glitters must necessarily be gold. Because of this, men who have had the reputation of being wise men in the world have recommended this to us as the greatest wisdom: **NOT TO BELIEVE EASILY**. <gloss>Be sober and remember to be skeptical: these are the sinews of the mind.</gloss> *Epicharmus* gained more credit for this one saying (and has perhaps done more good as well) than many who have been the authors of vast volumes. Now, if those things exposed to the senses—the proper objects of our eyes and ears—are subject to so much imposture and deceit that the wisest can barely know what to believe, how much more caution do we need in those things that are so far above the senses, and in some respects contrary to the senses (that is, *spirits*), so that we are not deceived? If we consider the nature of man—his bodily frame, the affections of his soul, the faculties of his mind—we shall have no reason at all to wonder why most men are inclined to believe and to be cheated. But while there is no cause to wonder, there is just as little reason to imitate them: *Felix qui rerum potuit cognoscere causas!* <note>Happy is he who is able to know the causes of things!</note> <term>τερατολογία</term>, *a desire for, or toward, strange things that may cause amazement*, is the characteristic passion of the common people—that is, of most men—which they bring into the world with them (it is the observation of the wisest men who have written concerning the affairs and actions of humanity) and cannot be rid of except through wisdom, which is the happiness of a few. *Errandi, non necessitas tantum, sed amor* <note>There is not only a necessity of erring, but a love for it</note>, as *Seneca* says somewhere when speaking of the nature of man. There was a time when the world was greatly governed by *oracles*; private individuals went to them as they would to God, and kings and princes sent to them to be advised about the greatest matters. So much faith was generally attributed to them that the very word became a proverb applicable to those things about which no question can be made. Yet those very same ancient heathens who tell us of these oracles also tell us of their vanity. And though they do not say that all were false and counterfeit, yet while they acknowledge it of some, they give us just occasion to suspect that it might have been found equally true of the rest as well, had similar care been taken to examine their truth.

Again, there was a time (and that time is not yet many hundred years past) when *miracles* were the only conversation and delight of men. Ghosts and spirits were in every house, and men were so prone to believe what was delivered to them in that category that miracle-makers were hard-pressed—not to make their stories probable (for that was not insisted upon), but to make them wonderful enough. This went so far that some have been forced <margin>See the Life of *Albertus Magnus*</margin> to complain publicly about the credulity of the people, though they themselves tell us much more, I dare say, than was ever true. As it was with miracles, so it was with *exorcisms*: How many devils and spirits have been driven out of men and women supposedly possessed, through solemn exorcisms, to the great wonder of the onlookers—only to be proved later, upon further search and examination, to have been nothing but the artifices and subtle contrivances of men? Verdicts and judgments have been passed upon such frauds when they have been discovered in most parts of *Europe*, and these have been published. Yet, some (who were thought to be possessed) have indeed done strange things, things that seem impossible to ordinary sense to be done by nature. It is very true, some have. But those who know what strange things may be done to the amaze-

# The PREFACE.

amazement of all those not acquainted with such mysteries; yet by long *use* and *custom*, they will not easily wonder (so as to turn it into a supernatural thing) even though they see things which, to their own sight and to that of most people, cannot but seem very wonderful and almost impossible. As for the bodily temperament of man and of his *brain*, it has been sufficiently proved by some recent books on that subject (*Enthusiasm*), both by arguments from nature and by various examples, that a very slight disorder of the brain—scarcely discernable to anyone except those who are well-versed in the study of natural causes—is enough to represent spirits, angels and devils, and sights and stories of heaven and hell to the imagination. By this sober kind of madness and delirium, so little understood by the common people, many have been and are daily deceived. From these things, through the ignorance of men, strange events have sometimes followed, and the peace of commonwealths has suffered not a little.

*Aristotle*, in his *Meteors*, tells of one who always saw (or so he thought, at least) another man's shape before his eyes; he gives a reason for how this happened to him naturally. *Hippocrates*, in <term>Περί παρθενίων</term> (a very short discourse, but full of excellent matter), shows how some, both men and women, through natural causes, come to imagine to themselves that they see <term>δαίμονας</term> (devils and spirits) and to be tormented in their souls, even to the point of killing themselves with their own hands. The author of the book *On the Sacred Disease* (very ancient too, but not actually *Hippocrates*, as many believe) has excellent material as well for the same purpose, but I do not have the book with me at this time. *Hippocrates* (in the place mentioned before) shows how many in that case were tricked by the priests of those times, who made them believe that this happened to them through the anger of some god.

Those who are well-versed in optics know that there is a way, with the help of hidden lenses, to make moving shadows that appear like ghosts, to the great terror of the ignorant beholder; and it is said that pretended astrologers and fortune-tellers cheat many with these sights. It is the opinion of some Jewish Rabbis that whatever ghosts or souls are raised by *necromancy*, they always appear *inverso corpore*—that is, with their heads downward and feet upward. Though nothing is to be wondered at in Rabbis—who (commonly) are as full of ridiculous ideas as ever came into the head of any madman—yet my opinion is that the first basis for this wild idea was some appearance by the <term>species</term> (visual images) of an object, gathered through a small lens into a dark room. For indeed, the objects must appear *inverso corpore* if it is done in a high room and the objects from which the images are gathered are lower than the glass through which they pass. The reason for this is easily demonstrated to the sight of any reasonable man. Certainly, by this secret (which is no great secret, being commonly seen and practiced among those who are at all curious), strange things may be done by a cunning man, to the great amazement of those who do not know the cause. There would be no end if I should attempt to gather from various authors what has been invented by men, and what may be done by art to cheat men in matters of this nature. Let any man who is still a stranger to it simply read the life of *Alexander* the false prophet, or prognosticator, written by *Lucian*, and he shall see notable examples of successful cheats and impostures—scarcely credible, indeed, were it not that the event was still fresh and famous at the time, and that all the circumstances of

# The PREFACE.

History confirms the truth of the account. And let those who read it judge what dull and dry fellows the mountebank-astrologers, prognosticators, and fortune-tellers of these days are compared to this noble, renowned *Alexander*. Only let the reader know that *Lucian* was a professed atheist, and therefore it is no wonder if he finds *Epicurus* spoken of with great respect, whom all atheists and those inclined toward atheism are so much obliged to honor. With this exception, I think the story is very worthy of being known, and much more worthy of being read by all people (considering the good use that may be made of it) than many books that are daily translated from other languages.

But lastly, if there were actually such things as devils and spirits that appear to people, to whom should they (probably) appear sooner than to those who daily call upon them and devote their souls and bodies to them by dreadful oaths and curses? And again, why would they not appear to those who, through damnable curiosity, have many times used the methods (the best they could find in books, by magical circles, characters, and invocations) and yet never—neither the one nor the other—saw anything?

I have said as much as I intend to say (though perhaps something might be added) to show the plausibility of this opinion in opposition to common understandings and abilities. By this (as I understand it, for I have not knowingly omitted anything I thought important), this opinion chiefly claims for itself wisdom and more than ordinary prudence, which all people generally desire. Yet I would not have it thought that all people who hold this conclusion—that there are no spirits, etc.—go about it so rationally, or can give this explanation or any other more rational and plausible reason for what they believe. God knows there are many in the world, people of no learning and small ability, who can speak as decisively as the best—not because they have considered it and understand the grounds of either opinion, but because they know, or have heard, that it is the opinion of some learned people, and they hope they shall be thought learned too if they agree with them. 

Besides an ordinary (for some have been learned) *Epicurean*, who makes it his motto (to himself and in his heart) <term>Ἐν τῷ μηδὲν εἰδέναι ἥδιστος βίος</term> <note>"In knowing nothing is the sweetest life"</note> and seeks his ease in this world (<term>ἀταραξίαν</term>, their own word, which means *tranquility* of both mind and body; a good word but poorly applied) as his <term>summum bonum</term>, or highest happiness. It is a great relief to him when any strange things happen by witches, wizards, and the like; while some others, to satisfy their faith, and others their reason and curiosity, are compelled to inquire of men through discussion and to search into books, both ancient and recent, sacred and profane—and even all that is barely enough. It is a great relief, I say, for him then, and on all such occasions, to keep his soul in secure ignorance and to save his reputation (and even to gain reputation with some) by merely saying, "*It is a fable; I do not believe it.*" 

We shall hear some of them acknowledge as much as I have said in a moment; I am not imposing anything on them. Now for the *Epicureans* (of all philosophers the most insignificant in matters of knowledge, as former ages have described them), no man need wonder if they denied those things which, by the solemn engagement of their sect, they were bound and resolved to disbelieve—or at least not to acknowledge—notwithstanding any sight or sense, experience or evidence to the contrary. This clearly appears by one who may be believed (though I have met with it in more) in such things: *Lucian* (himself a professed *Epicurean Atheist*), who commends *Democritus*, *Epicurus*, and *Metrodorus* (the most famous of that sect) for their *ἀδαμαντίνην γνώμην*, as he calls it—their *fixed, irrevocable, unconquerable resolution*. When they saw any strange thing that was admired by others as miraculous, if they could find the cause or give a probable guess, well and good; if not, they still refused to depart from their first resolution, and continued to believe and maintain that it was false and impossible. It is a notable passage, and one of which excellent use may be made. I will therefore set down his own words for the sake of those who understand the language: — ὥς πάνυ τὸ μηχάνημα

# The PREFACE.

(Besides the judgment of everyone considered wise and learned in previous ages), I am convinced in my own judgment that such a great amount of solid reason in all arts and sciences never came from any mortal man (known to us through his writings) without supernatural illumination. Well: *Aristotle* does not acknowledge spirits; he does not mention them anywhere. Let that be granted. And why should it be a surprise to anyone who knows the aim and purpose of *Aristotle*'s *philosophy*? He lived at the same time as *Plato*; he had been his fellow student under *Socrates*, and for some time he was *Plato's* student. But afterward, he became his rival and took great pleasure in opposing his doctrine, so much so that some ancient writers criticize him for his ingratitude. 

The truth is, *Plato*'s writings are full of marvels, apparitions of souls, the pains of hell and purgatory, revelations of the gods, and similar things. In these matters, he is so bold that he is often forced to excuse himself, and he does not expect anyone to believe him according to the literal word of his stories, but only in a general sense—that something of that nature was true. Indeed, he has many divine passages—even whole treatises—that can never be admired enough for what they are; but it cannot be denied that they are too full of tales for a philosopher. *Aristotle*, therefore, decided on a completely opposite approach: he would deal with nothing except what had some apparent basis in nature. It was not that he specifically denied all other things, but because he did not think it was the role of a philosopher to deal with matters for which no probable reason could be given. 

This clearly appears in a divine passage of his, *<term>De part. anim.</term> book 1, chapter 5*, where he divides substances into <term>ἀγεννήτους καὶ ἀφθάρτους</term>, *eternal and incorruptible*—which is, in effect, spiritual. (For even spirits that were created might be termed <term>ἀγέννητοι</term>, which strictly means *those that do not have their beginning through generation*; however, we will readily admit that the creation of angels, whether good or bad, was not known to *Aristotle*; we may instead understand these as gods and intelligences.) The other group consists of those that <term>μετέχουσι γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς</term>—that is, *are mortal*. 

He continues: "As for divine substances, which we honor, we can say but little of them, though we desire to, because so little of them is exposed to the senses [and reason]. Mortal things, with which we are familiarly acquainted and interact daily, we may know if we apply ourselves. But we should rejoice much more in the knowledge of divine things because of their excellence (even if we know only a very small part of them) than in the knowledge of these worldly things, however perfect and general that knowledge might be. But the comfort we have regarding mortal things (which compensates somewhat) is their certainty, and the fact that they fall within the scope of the sciences." 

What could be said more divinely by a man who had received nothing through revelation? Truly, it seems to me (if I may speak without causing offense or being misunderstood) that there is more divinity in those words than in some books that claim to be about nothing else. Add to this another passage in his *Metaphysics*, where he says that although supernatural things are clear and certain in themselves, they are not so to us, who see them only with "owls' eyes." <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics* 993b9-11: "For as the eyes of bats are to the blaze of day, so is the reason in our soul to the things which are by nature most evident of all."</note> Can we say then that *Aristotle* denied those things he refrained from writing about because their natures and qualities were beyond human knowledge? Nor is it absolutely true that *Aristotle* never wrote of spirits and apparitions. *Cicero*, in his first book *<term>De Divinatione</term>*, has a long story taken from him about a form or spirit that appeared in a dream to a certain *Eudemus* (his close friend and...

But on the other side, he says, it is no less hard to deny what all men, or most men, believe: namely, that there are such predictions. For to say (in his own words) that such dreams come from God—besides what else might be objected (which might easily be understood by those who understand his doctrine)—it is most unreasonable to believe that God would send them to men who are either vicious in their lives, or idiots and fools, the most vile and contemptible of all men, who have been observed to have such dreams more often than better and wiser men. So, leaving the matter undetermined, he proceeds to the consideration of those prophetic dreams for which some probable reason may be given.

Many other philosophers who have been of the greatest fame were certainly great magicians, such as *Orpheus*, *Pythagoras*, *Empedocles*, and the like, as may be gathered from those things that have been written about them by several ancient authors. But above all, I give the preeminence to *Apollonius Tyanaeus*, a man of later times, and of whom we may speak with more confidence and certainty. This was the man whom the ancient Heathens, very tenacious of their former worship and superstitions, chose to oppose Christ. His life has been written by several people; four of these accounts were joined together and opposed to the four Gospels. And *Hierocles*, a famous philosopher of those times, made a comparison of his miracles with those of Christ, and was answered by *Eusebius*, in a work still extant. And though they contain many fabulous things, as any man may expect from such an undertaking, yet they have so much truth and variety of ancient learning that I think they deserve to be better known than they commonly are; but they <unclear>cannot</unclear> be understood, I am sure, as they should be, by any translation, either Latin or French, that I have ever seen. The greatest wonder to me is that such was his bearing and outward appearance of sanctity and simplicity that even Christians have thought reverently of him and believed that he did his wonders by the power of God, or by secret philosophy and knowledge of nature not revealed to other men. I wonder very much whether any man who is a scholar and not strongly prejudiced—who does not believe in spirits, etc.—can say that he ever read the books of trials and confessions of witches and wizards, those, I mean, that have been written by learned and judicious men. Such as, for example, I consider *Nichol Remigius*, and his *Demonolatria: ex judiciis capitalibus 900 plus minus hominum, &c.* <note>Demonolatry: from the capital trials of 900 people, more or less, etc.</note> grounded especially upon the confessions and condemnations of no less than 900 men and women in *Lorraine* within the span of a few years. That he was a learned man, I think nobody who has read him will deny; and that he was not a very credulous or superstitious man (though a Papist), that also is most certain; and I have wondered at his freedom many times. I do not know how it is now in those places; but from what I have read and heard of the actions of witches and sorcerers in *Geneva* and *Savoy* in former times (I could say something of myself, how my life was preserved there very strangely, but my witnesses are not present, and I will not bring their reputation into question for such a matter), I am of the opinion that anyone there who would have maintained that there was no such thing as witches or spirits, etc., would have been thought by most to be either mad and brain-sick (so frequent and visible were the effects to sober eyes) or a witch himself. For indeed it is common enough that those who really are witches are very willing—which deceives many—to be thought impostors, and there is good reason for it. I would sooner suspect him to be an impostor who professes himself to be one (unless it is by way of confession, as many have done) and is ambitious to be considered a witch or sorcerer. 

I remember I saw a book some years ago entitled *De l’inconstance des mauvais Anges & Demons* <note>On the Inconstancy of Evil Angels and Demons</note>, printed at *Paris* in 1612 in quarto, and another by the same author and size entitled *L’incredulite & mescreauce du sortilege* <note>The Incredulity and Disbelief of Witchcraft</note>, *Paris 1642*. Strange stories are told there of a province of *France* around that time (or a little before) marvelously infested with witches and sorcerers, so much so that people did not recognize one another (in certain places) in the streets because of evil spirits appearing publicly in the shape of men; and that the proceedings of justice—which does not happen often—were sometimes disturbed by them. And indeed, it so happened once in Rome, as is recorded at large by *Pliny*. There, some ascribed such power to herbs as though the sun and moon were subject to them, the dead might be raised, armies vanquished, and what not! This was not very well received by many. At last came *Asclepiades*, who persuaded men (who were very well inclined to be persuaded) that all medicinal use of herbs and simples was a mere cheat, and that men were better off without them, there being other easier and less troublesome means to restore health and overcome diseases, which he professed to teach. He prevailed so far for a while that they were laid aside and a new course of medicine was introduced. There was in *Aix* (*Aquæ Sextiæ* anciently, now *Aquensis Civitas*) in *Provence* (a county of *France* so called) in the year of our Lord 1611, a Roman Catholic priest tried, convicted, and by sentence of the Court or Parliament condemned to be burned alive for abominable practices, and horrid things committed by him upon various people (some persons of quality) with and by the devil. I have been somewhat curious for someone of my calling, having no other goal but to attain some knowledge of nature—without which a man may quickly be led into manifold delusions and impostures. I have read some and looked into many; I do not remember meeting any professional physician or naturalist (except for one or two who have been or shall be named) who questioned these things. I am certain I have encountered various strange accounts in several of their works concerning things where they themselves were present and saw with their own eyes. In these cases, they could have no motive that any man could reasonably suspect other than to acknowledge the truth—even though it might bring some disparagement to themselves (in the judgment of many) through the free confession of their own ignorance and inability to provide reasons or penetrate into causes.

Yet it seems he was one of those who did not believe, or would not believe (though he does not say so positively), in Spirits and *Witches* and Supernatural Operations. What then? He plainly maintains and argues (though he quotes no Gospel for it) that such is the nature of the human soul (if one knows how to use it) that by a strong faith and confidence it may work any miracle without a miracle: *Verum confidentia illa, ac firma persuasio* (so that you may have some of his words if you do not have the book) *comparatur indoctis animis per opinionem quam de Characteribus & sacris verbis conceperunt. Regarding a strong confidence in God—even in those who are not otherwise very godly—and whether it might, according to God's original order and appointment, sometimes produce some strange effects: we have considered this elsewhere, where we treat of *Prayer-based Enthusiasm* <note>Precatorie Enthusiasm</note>. But to conclude this part; upon due consideration of the premises, and what else I have in readiness upon the same subject (if God gives me life and health), I cannot satisfy myself how any learned man, sober and rational, can entertain such an opinion (simply and seriously) *That there are no Devils nor Spirits, etc.* I can only account for it this way (leaving all men to their own judgments in this): if there truly and really are such people, it must be because, having been at first biased by some plausible ground and being afterwards occupied with other thoughts and employments, they are more willing to stick to their former opinion without further trouble than to take the pains to seek further. *Οὕτως ἀταλαίπωρος τοῖς πολλοῖς ἡ ζήτησις τῆς ἀληθείας, καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἕτοιμα μᾶλλον τρέπονται* <note>"So little pains do most people take in the search for truth, and they turn rather to what is ready at hand."</note>, as *Thucydides* does very well observe. And when we say, *A Learned man*, there is much ambiguity in that word. For a man may be—not to speak of the ignorance of the common people, especially in those climates where they think all learning is contained in preaching; and now in these times, too, they consider those the best preachers who in very deed have the least learning, but preach by "instinct" and "inspiration," as they call it—but a man, I say, may be a *Learned Man*, a very *Learned man* in some one field or profession, even to excellence and admiration, who nevertheless is and may be found ignorant enough in other fields. But a generally learned man is a thing of a vast extent, and not often seen. It is a business of infinite labor, besides requiring matching natural abilities; without which (especially judgment), the more pains one takes, sometimes the more ignorance results. I do not aim this at any particular man or men (*I call God to witness*); I would much rather submit myself to the censure of others than take it upon me to censure anyone. But the observation is of very good use, I know it, and it may give much satisfaction in many cases; I have given an instance of it in *Tertullian*, and some others elsewhere.

I have finished for this time; I come now to the Objections, where I shall not need to be very long, because they run much upon one thing, Imposture, which has already been spoken of and answered. But yet something more particularly shall be answered.

First, *Of Miracles*. It cannot be denied that the world is full of horrible impostures in that particular. Yet I believe that some supernatural things, such as cures, etc., do happen in every age for which no reason can be given, and which also for their strangeness may be called miracles. I hope I shall do no wrong to the memory of that venerable, incomparable prelate, **BISHOP ANDREWES**—renowned for sound learning and true piety while he lived, and one of the greatest lights of this land—if I set down two stories, which we may call *miracles*. He believed both of these to be true, and for one of them, it seems, he vouched for it based on his own knowledge. The first concerns a noted, or at least widely suspected, witch or sorceress, whom the Devil, in a strange shape, attended (or rather waited for) at her death. The other concerns a man who, after his death, was restored to life to confess a horrible murder committed upon his own wife, for which he had never been suspected. He related both of these to my father <note>Méric Casaubon's father, Isaac Casaubon</note> in familiar conversation, and my father entered them as a record into some of his *notebooks* <note>Adversaria</note>. In substance, I believe there could be no mistake, but if there is any error in the circumstances, such as names or otherwise, that must be attributed to my father, who was a stranger not only to the language but to all the affairs of England (beyond what might be known through printed books and other public means).

->The First, thus:<-

### *L., an old woman of London, whom the Devil attended at her death.*

*A wonderful story which the Lord Bishop related as being very well known to him. There was a certain woman, L., very wealthy and highly addicted to the occult arts. She was a neighbor to the house of Fulke, who was the father of Lord Fulke, famous throughout all England; she was also very intimate with that same distinguished matron, the mother of Fulke. This woman was devoted to sorcery throughout her whole life, and for that reason was a friend and patroness of infamous women. When she was dying, and several very serious men and women were present, it was noticed around the hour of death that a man of terrible appearance, clothed in fox skins, stood at the foot of the bed. She stared at him with intense eyes, and he at her. The doorkeeper was asked why he had let him in; he denied that he had even seen him. Finally, two or three withdrew to the window to decide what they should do with him. There was a certain Senator of great reputation... who was twice Lord Mayor of London; also the father of Fulke, and others. They decided to address him and ask who he was. With this intention, they returned to their places at the bedside. Meanwhile, L. let out a loud cry, as if she were giving up the ghost; everyone attended to her, watched her, and lifted her up. Soon she came to herself, and they looked for that unknown man. He appeared nowhere. Within an hour's time, the sick woman died.*

In that street is a parish and a parish house, in which there was a priest, a man of the highest faith and noted piety... in the year 1563, a year in which the plague raged through this city of London as much as ever. This parish priest told many people, and the Lord Bishop himself, that this had happened to him. He had a distinguished friend in his parish, a man whom everyone considered honest and pious. This man, seized by the plague, called for that priest, his friend, who attended to him while he was sick, saw him dying, and did not leave until he was dead; only then did he return to his own home. Many hours after his death, while he was left as a corpse in his bedroom, his wife entered the same room to take a shroud or linen cloth from a chest to <gloss>shroud</gloss> him, as is the custom. Having entered, and intent on her task, she heard this voice: *Who is here?* She was terrified and wanted to leave, but she heard that voice again: *Who is here?* At last, realizing it was her husband's voice, she went to him: "What," she said, "husband; are you then not dead? We had laid you out as dead and left you." "Indeed," he replied, "*I was truly dead; but it seemed good to God that my soul should return to my body. But you, wife,* he said, *if you have any food prepared, give it to me, for I am hungry.*" She said she had mutton, chicken, and some other things, but everything was uncooked, though she would prepare it shortly. "I cannot bear the delay," he said; "*do you have bread and cheese?*" When she said yes and he asked for it to be brought, he ate while his wife watched. Then, having called for the priest and ordered everyone present to leave the bedroom, he told him this: "*I was truly dead,*" he said, "*but my soul was ordered to return to its body so that I might reveal with my mouth a crime committed by my hands, for which no one ever had any suspicion. For I myself killed my first wife with my own hands, with such cunning that the whole matter remained hidden.*" Then he explained the manner in which the crime was committed; not long after, he expired and was then truly dead.

There is no necessity for anyone to make an article of faith out of either of these stories; yet I thought them very probable because they were believed by such a man, and therefore I have given them a place here. So much for *miracles*.

Of *exorcisms*, we must say the same as we say of *miracles*. We have one notable example of a counterfeit possession, and of the great unrest likely to have followed it in *France*, from *Thuanus* in our recent *Treatise on Enthusiasm*. The history of the *Boy of Bilson* is well known; he was discovered to be an impostor, specifically set up and bribed to promote the Roman Catholic cause in the year 1620, through the wisdom and sagacity of the Right Reverend Father in God *Thomas*, Lord Bishop of *Lichfield* and *Coventry*. Most countries have produced a good supply of such examples and stories, which are available in various languages. Nor must it be hidden (by those who seek truth without partiality) that some, once called *Disciplinarians* but now better known by another name, have attempted to involve themselves in these matters, hoping thereby to gain a great advantage for their cause. It was a famous story in Queen Elizabeth’s reign—though now perhaps forgotten by many and beyond the memory of anyone living—how one Mr. *D.*, a very zealous man of that sect, took it upon himself through long prayers to cast out devils. This was maintained and asserted with great vehemency by him and others who favored that cause, though upon legal examination they were proved otherwise. This occasioned many books on both sides in those days, but two of *better note*, as we say, were written by Dr. *H.* concerning *exorcisms*: one against the Papists and the other against *P.* I still have them both somewhere, I hope, but I cannot get to

I would judge charitably, even of those men who are not very charitable toward others, whose judgments and consciences will not allow them (though they are men of proven worth and piety otherwise) to say what they say and do what they do in all things.

...were the deceptions of men. Sometimes Princes, sometimes private men (as now regarding religion, preaching, praying, and fasting; of Masses and processions: most Princes and States in all places) made good use of them for their own ends, and made them speak what they themselves had prompted. But a man might just as probably argue that because some have been so freely acknowledged to have been created by conspiracy and bribery, it is the more likely that those of which there was never any suspicion should be true. We read of many in *Herodotus*: of one which was contrived by fraud; but there we also read that when it became known (though care had been taken that it might not be), the chief contriver, a great man, was banished—or avoided worse by a voluntary exile—and the *Sacred Virgin* or *Prophetess* was deposed. 

But not to insist upon particulars, which would take too long, it is most certain—and it will clearly appear to those who are well-read in ancient authors and histories—that all heathens, generally the wisest and most learned of them (especially those who lived when oracles were most frequent), did really believe them to be what they claimed to be. And that they were so indeed, for the most part (taking it for granted that their gods were *devils* or *evil spirits*), may be made just as evident by many circumstances in stories and by other good proofs. Neither was it ever doubted or denied by ancient Christians—I am sure by most, if not all—though it was always granted and presupposed that, as in all worldly things, much imposture did intervene and intermingle. But I have spoken of them elsewhere already, and therefore will be briefer here.

Our last objection was: if there are devils and spirits, why do they not appear to those who do what they can—whether by continual curses or by profane curiosity—to invite them? First, we say, *ἀνεξερεύνητα τὰ κρίματα αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνεξιχνίαστοι αἱ ὁδοὶ αὐτοῦ* <note>Romans 11:33: "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!"</note>. When we have good ground for the <term>ὅτι</term> (the fact that it is so), to hesitate at the <term>διότι</term> (the reason why) because we do not understand the reason, is as much as to say that we think we should be as wise as God. *Aristotle* did not meddle with things for which he could give no reason; yet he did not deny them (as we have shown). It is one thing to require a reason for things that are purely natural, and another for those that happen by a purely secret Providence. But this will give little satisfaction to those who perhaps believe in a God only as much as they believe in a devil. 

Secondly, therefore, we say there may be some natural reason too, based on *Aristotle’s* grounds. *Aristotle* (as has been shown elsewhere) compares the effects of melancholy—from which he derives all kinds of *enthusiasm*—to the known effects of *wine*. What is the reason that some men, with little wine, will quickly become drunk and turn into other creatures, being deprived for the time of the use of reason? Others, though they drink ever so much, will sooner burst than reel or speak idly. Just as some in their excess grow merry and others sad; some calm and better-natured, others furious; some talkative, others stupid. The devil knows what temperaments are best for his purposes; and from some by whom he was deceived, he has gained no credit and wished he had never meddled with them. Some men come into the world with *cabalistic brains*; their heads are full of mysteries; they see nothing, they read nothing, but their brain is at work to pick something out of it that is extraordinary. Reason and sense, which other men follow, they think of as the acorns that the ancient world fed upon; fools and children may be content with them, but they see into things by another *Light*. They commonly respect the *Scriptures* (until they come to profess themselves *Anabaptists*) because they believe them to be the Word of God and not of men; but they reserve the interpretation for themselves, and so, under the title of Divine Scripture, they worship whatever their own fancy prompts or the devil puts into their heads. But of all Scriptures, the *Revelation* and the obscure prophecies are their delight; for there they wander securely; and there is nothing so prodigious or chimerical that they cannot extract it from some prophecy, as they choose to interpret it. These men, if they are upright in their lives and dealings and truly fear God, it is to be hoped that God will preserve them from further evil; but they are of a dangerous temperament; charitable men will pity them, and sober men will avoid them. On the other hand, there are some whose brains are of a stiff and stubborn mold; they do not easily receive new impressions. They will hardly believe anything but what they see; and yet they would rather not believe their eyes than believe anything that is not according to the course of nature and what they have been used to. The devil may tempt such people with sensual baits and catch them; but he will not easily attempt to delude them with magical shows and apparitions. And what sober man, who believes in a God and a devil alike, doubts that those who make it their daily practice to damn themselves with such horrid oaths and curses are just as truly possessed—indeed, far more in the possession of the devil—than many who foam at the mouth and speak strange languages?

But 3rdly, some have tried and used these means but could never see anything. Yet what if others who never really desired it, but acted out of some reckless curiosity—unadvisedly, perhaps so that they might be better able to refute the simplicity of others (as they thought), rather than because their faith needed any such confirmation—have tried certain things or have been present at some experiments and have seen (to no small astonishment) more than they expected or desired? Some persons of credit and quality, I am sure, have confessed to me that it has happened so to them; they were so affected by it that they would not for the world be so surprised again.

But 4thly and lastly, the confessions of some magicians are available in print; they tell very specifically what means they used, what books they read, etc., and they saw and found things (if we believe them—and I do not know what should tempt them to lie, as they were not melancholy men) until they were weary, and God's grace worked upon their hearts to bring them to repentance. Such confessions exist, but the reader shall pardon me if I give him no further account. It would much better become those, therefore, who have made such attempts without success, to repent and to be thankful to God, rather than to use that as an argument that there is no devil and perhaps no God. There is a terrible saying (if well understood) in the Scripture: "ὁ ῥυπῶν ῥυπάτω, *He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.*" Let them take heed (I advise them as a friend), if they persist in their hardness of heart and infidelity, lest God in just judgment—though they still seek and provoke as much as they can—will not allow them to see anything, lest they should fear and be converted.

# THE PREFACE.

I come now to Dr. **Dee**, and to *this book* of his, which has been the occasion of all the discourse so far. As for his person or parentage, education, and the like, I have little more to say than what he says himself in his first letter to the Emperor (*Rodolphe*) of *Germany*: that while still very young, he was sought after (*ambiverunt me*) by two Emperors, *Charles* V and *Ferdinand*, his brother and successor in the Empire. Mr. *Camden* indeed, in the year 1572, makes honorable mention of him and calls him a '*Noble Mathematician*'. He dedicated his *Monas Hieroglyphica* to *Maximilian*, successor to *Ferdinand*; it was first printed at *Antwerp* in the year of our Lord 1564, and afterwards at *Frankfurt* in 1591, and I know not where else. In the year 1595, he wrote (and it was certainly printed in 1599, though I cannot say if it was printed before then) *A Discourse Apologetical*, etc., directed to the then *Archbishop of Canterbury*. In it, he has a catalogue of books written by himself, both printed and unprinted, totaling 48 in all; he also mentions the books in his library, about 4000 volumes in total, of which 700 were ancient manuscripts in *Latin*, *Greek*, and *Hebrew*. There he also produces a testimony from the *University of Cambridge*, dated 1548. But this entire discourse of his being short, for the reader's better satisfaction, I thought it good to have it reprinted here immediately following this preface. His *Mathematical Preface* to *Euclid* is, I think, the work of all his published writings that has been most noticed in *England*, and it added much to the worth and praise of that edition of *Euclid*. He was a married man and had various children, as will appear by this *Relation*; he was a great traveler and lived to a great age. But as I said before, I do not pretend to give others an account of his life in general, which I myself am still a stranger to. I am to give an account regarding what concerns this *Relation*, and I hope nothing shall be lacking in that. To that end, I propose four things to myself:

*First*, to somewhat confirm the truth and sincerity of this entire *Relation*.

*Secondly*, to answer some objections that may be made against parts of it.

*Thirdly*, to clarify certain passages and to satisfy the reader concerning the perfection and imperfection of the book, as well as the original copy.

*Fourthly*, and lastly, to show the many good uses that a sober Christian may make of it all.

I. It seems that Dr. **Dee** began to have the reputation of a *conjurer* early on. For my part, I still question whether he could ever truly be called such a thing; but I am very confident that he himself did not know or think himself so, but rather a zealous worshiper of God and a very free and sincere Christian. # The PREFACE.

Nobody will so grossly mistake us as though we intended thereby to justify what is printed here against any suspicion of forgery, as if any man, taking the advantage of *Dr. Dee's* name and fame as a *conjurer*, could be suspected to have devised and invented these things in his own brain to abuse the world. I would be sorry for my name to appear in any way in any book liable to such a suspicion; and the very name and credit of that so much and so deservedly prized *Library* from which this is claimed to be taken is sufficient (among civil, understanding men) to prevent the grossness of such a mistake. Besides, the Original Copy itself, all written in *Dr. Dee's* own hand, is kept and preserved there. But by *Truth* and *Sincerity*, I intend not only *Dr. Dee's* fidelity in relating what he himself believed, but also the reality of those things that he speaks of, according to his account: his only (but great and dreadful) error being that he mistook false, lying spirits for *Angels of Light*, the *Devil of Hell* (as we commonly call him) for the *God of Heaven*. For the *Truth* then, and *Sincerity* or *Reality* of the *Relation* in this sense, I shall first appeal to the *Book* itself. I know it is the fashion of many (I will not say that I never did it myself) who buy books to turn five or six pages; if they happen upon something that pleases their fancy, the book is a good book, and when they have bought it, it concerns them to think so because they have paid for it. But on the other side, if they happen upon something that does not please (which may happen in the best of books), they are just as ready to condemn and cast it away. It is very possible that some such buyer, happening upon this work and finding in it some places here and there where some odd, uncouth things may appear—things ridiculous or incredible to ordinary sense and understanding—he may be ready to judge the whole accordingly. But despite all this, I will in the first place appeal to the book itself; but with this request to the Reader: that he will have the patience to read in order at least one-fourth of the book before he judges; and if by that time he is not convinced, he shall have my permission to give it up. But then to the Emperor *Rudolph*, to *Stephen*, King of *Poland*, and various other princes and their deputies—the wisest and most learned their several courts could provide at the time; the particulars of all these addresses and transactions are very exactly set down in the book. Indeed, such was his confidence that had it not been for the *Apostolic Nuncio* appearing against him at the Emperor's court by order from the Pope, he was—as may be gathered from some passages—resolved for *Rome* also, not doubting that he should justify himself and his actions to the Pope himself and his Cardinals. In all these addresses and applications, he was always very ready to impart all things to those who would receive them with the respect he thought they deserved; yes, and—what is very notable—readily even to receive into this "Mystical Society" those whom he thought worthy and in some capacity to promote the design. As a matter of fact, he did so with several people in various places: *Albertus Alasco*, Prince Palatine of *Poland*; *Puccius*, a learned man; and Prince *Rosemberg* in *Germany*, who were long members of the Society, besides some admitted to certain "actions" for a while, such as *Stephen*, King of *Poland*, and some others. We will easily grant (as has been discussed and handled at length elsewhere) that a disordered brain may see, yes, and hear strange things, and accept them with all possible confidence as real things, yet all be but fancy without any real sound or apparition. But these sights and apparitions of which Dr. *Dee* gives an account here are of quite another nature; yes, even though the Devil might possibly represent various things of this sort to the imagination internally

That these things could not be the operation of a disturbed imagination will be sufficient evidence to any rational person.

And again, his humility, piety, and patience—O, what a pity that such a man should fall into such a delusion! And truly, except for this one thing (as we said before)—his mistaking of evil spirits for good ones—it does not appear from anything else but that he kept his understanding and the perfect use of his reason to the very last, as well as he had at any other time of his life.

Again, consider that wherever he went, he carried with him A STONE, which he called his *Angelical Stone*, claiming it was brought to him by an angel (though certainly by a spirit). He showed this stone to many people, including the Emperor, or the Emperor's deputy, *Dr. Curtz*, as I recall. But more about this stone later. We may therefore conclude with enough certainty that *Dr. Dee* acted with complete simplicity and sincerity throughout this entire account. I shall only add that while I used the word *reality* earlier concerning the things that appeared in this account, I would not want to be misunderstood. I do not mean that whatever the Devil seemed to do or represent was *actually* and *substantially* as it appeared; that would be a great and gross mistake. The very word *apparition* implies the opposite. All I mean by *reality* is that the things which appeared did so by the power and operation of spirits who were actually present and working; they were not the effects of a depraved fancy or an imagination caused by purely natural means. I admit that through such imagination, strange things may be presented and perceived with total confidence by the people involved, as we said before, even though it is all just fantasy. ## II. Now to Objections:
The first shall be this: Although it is very probable that Dr. Dee himself acted simply and sincerely, yet since he himself saw nothing (for he admits this in some places) except through *Kelly’s* eyes, and heard nothing but with his ears, is it not possible that *Kelly*, being a cunning man and well-practiced in these things, might impose upon the credulity of Dr. Dee (a good, innocent man)? This is especially likely because, by this office under the Doctor, he earned 50 *l.* <note>pounds</note> per year, as it appears. Truly, this is plausible as it is proposed, and likely enough that it might carry great weight with those who are easily swayed, and therefore seldom see the truth or true nature of a thing, but only its outward appearance. But read and observe it diligently, and you will find it far otherwise. It is true indeed that ordinarily Dr. Dee did not see things himself; his business was to write what was seen (though in his presence) and heard by *Kelly*. Yet it often appears in many places that he himself heard things immediately; I shall not need any quotations for that which he feels as well as *Kelly*. In the account of the *Holy Stone*, how it was *taken away by one who came in through a window in the shape of a man, and how it was restored*; both certainly *saw* this. In the story of the *Holy Books, how they were burned and how they were restored again* (at least part of them), which Dr. Dee considered a great miracle, as appears by some of those places; there also both certainly saw it. And *Albert Lasky*, the *Polish Palatine, saw* as well as *Kelly*. Besides, it clearly appears throughout the whole book that *Kelly* (though sometimes persuaded with much effort for a while to think better of them) generally held no other opinion of these apparitions except that they were mere illusions of the Devil and evil spirits, such as he himself could command by his art whenever he wished, and was acquainted with. Indeed, we find him for this very reason leaving, or desiring to leave, Dr. Dee, who was much troubled by it and was forced in one place to *pawn his soul* to him (to use his own words) that it was not so, and that they were good spirits sent from God in great favor to them. But for all this, *Kelly* would not be satisfied, but insisted that his declaration or protestation of his suspicion to the contrary be entered into the book; you shall find this, and it will be worth your reading. Truly, if a man considers the whole conduct of this business from beginning to end, according to this true and faithful (for I think I may say so with confidence) account of it presented here to us, one sees how this poor man was from time to time shamefully and grossly delayed, deluded, and quarreled with without cause, yet still led on with some shows and appearances, and yet still frustrated and put off. Considering his many pangs and agonies about it, and his sad condition after so many years of toil, travel, drudgery, and earnest expectation at the very last (as appears by the *Actions and apparitions of the year 1607*), I cannot tell whether I should make him an object of more horror or compassion. Certainly, he deserves both in great measure from any man who has any sense of humanity or any regard for the examples of human frailty in others—and again, any regard for talent and worth, such as were in this man to a high degree. 

It is true that he had joys and comforts as well; they were imaginary and delusory, it is true, yet he enjoyed them and they kept up his heart and often made him outwardly cheerful, I have no doubt. These are the kinds of joys that the "Saints" (as they call themselves) and schismatics of these and former times have always been very prone to boast of, persuading themselves that they are the effects of God's blessed Spirit. But even in these joys and comforts—the fruits and fantasies of his deluded soul (as in many others with a distempered brain)—is he not an object of great compassion to anyone who is both sober and charitable? If this then were indeed his case, what shall we say? If nothing else, I believe it ought to satisfy a rational, sober, humble man to say: It is not in man’s power to give an account of all God’s judgments, nor is there any ground for us to murmur because we do not understand them, or because they often seem contrary...

And what do we think should put him upon such a desire, with hopes to obtain it, but an opinion he had of himself as an extraordinary man, both for *parts* and for *favor with God?* But however, had he been everything he could think of himself, besides his spiritual pride in thinking so of himself (as great a sin as any in the eyes of God), his praying for such a thing with so much importunity was a great tempting of God and deserving of the greatest judgments. Had he indeed been a suitor to God for such *Wisdom* as the Prophet *Jeremie* describes (*11. v. 24, 25.*) *Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, etc., but let him that glories, etc.* And for such knowledge as our Savior commands, *John 17:3: And this is life eternal, that they may know you, etc.* And his blessed Apostle (*1 Cor. 11:2*): *For I determined not to know anything, etc.*—he would have had good warrant for his prayers, and it is very likely that God would have granted him his request, as far as it might have concerned his own salvation and eternal happiness. Besides, it is lawful (even fitting) for a man to pray for God’s blessing upon his labors, and for a competency of wit and capacity so that he may do well in his vocation and glorify God. 

But for a man to aspire to such eminence above other men, and by means that are not ordinary (such as that conceited *Philosopher’s Stone* and the like), and to involve God by earnest solicitations in his ambitious, extravagant desires—that God who has said of himself *that he resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble*—must necessarily be so great and so high a provocation (if well considered) that I begin to doubt whether it is charity to pity him who suffered so justly and deservedly. I do not know but that it is just as lawful for any man born obscurely to pray for a kingdom, for a common soldier to pray that he may have strength to encounter thousands, or for an ordinary maid to pray that she may become the fairest of women. # The PREFACE.

We grant that it is possible to glorify God through all these things, if it were appropriate for us to dictate to God how He should be glorified while neglecting the means He has appointed; and if we could ensure that in claiming to seek God's glory, we are not actually seeking our own. I wish that our great innovators and reformers of the arts and sciences (at least, such is the wisdom they believe they have) would seriously consider this; especially those who take it upon themselves to make all men wise and of one mind, and to reconcile all doubts and difficulties in religion and other matters; in short, to make Truth embraced by all men. If these men were to tell us that had they been responsible for the creation of the world and the ordering of all things from the beginning (and I believe there are some in the world who have said almost as much), they would have made a different sort of world than God has done, we might perhaps consider what could be the basis for such incredible confidence in any mortal man. 

But since the condition of the world and of men is as it is—naturally speaking, or as a Christian would say, since the fall of *Adam* and its consequences, the curse of God, etc.—the idea of making all men wise, like-minded, good, and religious without an infinite, omnipotent power (the kind that was able to create a world out of nothing) is absurd. Can any sober and wise man hear such a thing—hear it with patience—when he would think it impossible, even strange, for castles to be built in the air or for the heavens to be attacked with cannons? And yet such books are read; yes, and highly valued by some men. In my judgment, those who boast of such things are to be pitied if mental imbalance is the cause (as I believe it is for some); but if they are clever and calculating, acting to gain reputation and money (as I believe some are), it is a strong testament to their confidence that there are many in the world who are not very wise. 

But to return to *Dr. Dee*: It might be further added and proved by examples that some men of extraordinary holiness and self-denial (in the eyes of men)—some so secluded from the world and its vanities that for many years they had, in a manner, conversed with God alone—nevertheless fell into delusions and temptations through pride and conceit regarding their own abilities and favor with God. These delusions, if not exactly the same as his, were no less strange and dreadful. Church history and other books of that nature will provide such examples, but I do not have them with me at the moment, and I believe I have said enough regarding this specific point.

But something should also be observed regarding his *praying*. *His spirits* tell him somewhere that he had the *gift of prayer*. I truly believe he did, in the way the term is commonly used: that is, he could express himself very fluently and earnestly in prayer, and he did so often to his own great satisfaction. Let no man wonder at this; I have shown elsewhere that some who have been very wicked—even some who died for blasphemy, with blasphemy on their lips until their last breath—have possessed this gift to a great degree and caused much mischief with it. This is no insult to prayer, any more than it is to the best things in the world (and what is better and more heavenly than prayer well used?) if they are abused. And it is commonly observed that the corruption of the best things is the most dangerous. What produced those destructive heretics who troubled the world for so long, and could not be suppressed except by total destruction, but long, performative prayers (for which they were called *Euchites* or *Messaliani*, that is to say, the *Prayers*) and *enthusiasms*? For when young boys and illiterate men (and their number is likely to increase now that <term>Catechizing</term> is so much neglected) are turned loose to exercise themselves in this "gift" (as they call it), and when by long practice they have attained to some readiness and fluency, which does cause some inward lightheartedness and excitement, or perhaps something that may have some resemblance to spiritual sorrow and remorse, they immediately think themselves inspired; and so they become "Saints" before they know what it is to be Christians. 

And if they can pray by <term>inspiration</term>, why not preach also? Thus comes in <term>Anabaptism</term> by degrees, which will be the ruin of all religion and civil government wherever it prevails. 

And I believe that this foolish, misguided notion of <term>inspiration</term>, just as it has been the cause of much other mischief, so also has it caused that horrid sacrilege—shall I call it, or profanation (I hope I may do either without offense, for it is not done by any public authority that I know of)—the casting out and banishing of <term>The Lord's Prayer</term> from many private houses and churches; than which, I think, Christ never received a greater insult from any who called themselves Christians. 

I am not so uncharitable as to believe that it is done in direct opposition to Christ by any real Christians, but rather out of a furious zeal, I believe, by many against set prayers. But this is not a place to dispute it. Certainly, as <term>The Lord's Prayer</term> is a prayer of most incredible comfort to those who use it devoutly and upon good grounds (meaning a good foundation of religion and sound faith), so I believe that set prayers in general are of more importance to the settling of peace in the commonwealth than many men realize. But let this stand as my opinion; I am sure there are worse ones that currently pass for truth.

And some write that until his dying day (having lived to the age of 80 years), he never recanted. 

And was this not the case of the learned *Postellus*, who fell into some grievous, wild fancies in his later days? Though he remained sound enough in other matters, he could never be reclaimed, even though the best and gentlest means (out of respect for his worth and person) that could be thought of were used from time to time. But what do we say of particular men? Consider the *Anabaptists* in general. Over a hundred years ago, they troubled *Germany* very much; it cost many thousands their lives. They roved up and down. No sooner were they destroyed in one place than they sprang up (while that season lasted) in another. Their pretenses everywhere were the same: *Revelations* and the *Spirit*; the wickedness of Princes and Magistrates; and *Christ Jesus* to be set up on His Throne. Well, at last, they were destroyed in most places. Stories of them have been written in all languages and read everywhere, as has their lamentable end. Can all this prevent them from starting up again in the same shape and form as before upon every opportunity of a confused and confounded Government? They use the same pretenses, the same *Scriptures*—for all the world, miserably distorted and abused—to raise tumults and seditions in all places. Such is the wretchedness of man once he is out of the right way of reason and sobriety. 

But at the same time, we must say in this particular case of *Dr. Dee’s*, though his obstinacy was great and marvelous, yet it must be acknowledged that the diligence and subtlety of his *Spirits* to keep their hold was great. Some things occasionally happened (such as his danger and preservation near *Gravesend* when he first went out of the realm, as related here) very strangely. Such was the unhappiness of his misapplied zeal that he saw a Providence in whatever happened to him as he desired.

Before either of them was born, the **BOOK OF ENOCH** was well known in the world; and at that time *Lingua Adami* (the Adamic language, upon which most of the <term>Cabala</term> stands) was also much discussed, as appears in the learned books of *Gregory of Nyssa* against *Eunomius* the Heretic. # The Preface.

...a much better Christian, by far, who does not regard it or desire it. For my part, although I must acknowledge that some doubts in my mind induced me to look into many books until I was satisfied—which otherwise I had never done—yet I profess to believe that there is so little that can be known by man on this subject, and it is subject to so much illusion, that I think no study is more vain and foolish. I would not go three steps out of my doors (more than what I did to satisfy my mind in some matters of faith, if any such doubt arose) to know as much as the profoundest Platonist, philosopher, or even magician among them all ever knew.

Certainly he is but a weak Christian—when so many high mysteries of such great consequence are proposed to us in Christ by his Gospel—who cannot spend his time better. Will those who have any hope, through faith in Christ and a godly life, to be admitted one day into the presence of God and to see him face to face, as God has promised, hazard so glorious a hope by prying through unreasonable and unprofitable curiosity into the nature of these vassal spirits, which God has forbidden?

But because it concerns religion in general that we believe in *spirits*, and when objections are made that cannot be answered, many are offended and atheists are ready to take advantage of it, I say that it should be no wonder to any sober and rational person if we cannot resolve all doubts. Since it is so little that we know, or can know, beyond the bare ὅτι <note>Greek for "the fact that something is," as opposed to its nature or cause</note> in this matter.

Most Christians are raised in this opinion: that all spirits (as they are commonly called) are either angels of heaven or devils of hell. I know of no Scripture for it, or any decree of any general council that I recall—at least at this time—and so long as that is the case, I do not think myself bound to it against apparent reason. As for the notion of all evil *spirits or devils being in hell*, I think the learned Mr. *Meade* has taken that to task in some of his works and sufficiently refuted it.

The very word *spirit* is a term of great ambiguity; we commonly understand it to mean substances that are altogether immaterial. It is well known that many of the ancient Fathers did not allow for any such beings at all, except for God. But we think that having no visible body and being purely immaterial are one and the same. God knows how many degrees there may be between these, but we cannot know it, nor does it concern our salvation, for which we have reason to praise God.

But if it were so, that all spirits are either devils or angels, what shall we make of those that are found in mines, of which the learned *Agricola* has written; or of those that have been called κόβαλοι <note>kobali</note> (from which probably, as we have said elsewhere, the English word *goblin* is derived) since time out of mind, who live in private houses, around old walls and stacks of wood? They are otherwise harmless but very thievish, and are so frequent and well-known in some countries that a man might as well doubt whether there are any horses in England because there are none in some parts of the world—they were not found in all of America, I think, until some were carried there.

Neither can I believe that those spirits that please themselves in nothing else but harmless sports and playfulness—such as have been known in all ages; such as used to shave the hair of *Plinius Secundus's* servants in the night, as he himself relates (a very credible man, I am sure) in his epistles, and the like—that such spirits, I say, have any relation to either heaven or hell. We might insist on more details, but we do not desire to dwell upon it at this time; and there is yet something else to be said. And

# The Preface.

Regarding what I have said about some Platonists, I did not intend thereby to justify all their absurd or superstitious opinions on the subject of spirits. As they have searched further into it than others (besides their dangerous experience, having mixed magic with philosophy, and indeed almost turned all philosophy into magic), it was inevitable that they would fall into more errors and absurdities; yet at the same time, they have found some things that agree better with daily experience than what is commonly known or believed. *Synesius* was a bishop, but as he appears to us in his writings, he was more of a Platonist than a Christian. In one passage (in his treatise *De insomniis* <note>On Dreams</note>), he shows how evil spirits come to inhabit men and possess their brains. His terms are very coarse and apparently ridiculous, but there may be some truth in the opinion. *For if there were not a very near and intimate conjunction, it would be a wonder how the Devil comes to know the very thoughts of witches and magicians, as is found by experience and affirmed by more than one person. And in this very book, if I am not mistaken, something may be observed to that purpose: it is possible there may be more kinds of possession than one, and that some men, who were never suspected, have had a spirit (besides their own) resident in them for all or most of their lives.*

I have finished with what I could think of upon which objections might be made. The next thing is to make the way clearer to the reader by some consideration of the *method of the books* and an explanation of some terms and phrases used there, which perhaps some may find difficult at first. At the very beginning, a man may be confused by the title: *Liber sexti mysteriorum, & sancti parallelus, novalisque. 1583.* <note>The book of the sixth of the mysteries, both parallel and new, 1583</note>, both in how it relates to what follows and how it *reflects* upon something that came before, from which it may be inferred that the book begins here abruptly and imperfectly. I am now ready to give an account of this to the reader, and it is very fitting that it should be done.

First, concerning titles—of which many more will be found here besides this, the whole book or relation being subdivided into many parts—I say in general that according to the Doctor's nature (we said before he was very *Cabalistic*, that is, full of whimsical and eccentric ideas under the notion of mysteries, something that some otherwise very able men have been subject to) and the high opinion he had of these actions and apparitions, they are mostly very concealed and (to speak the truth) fantastic, which must make them more obscure. I could give the reader a view of them all here put together, but it would be superfluous. There are some fourteen or fifteen divisions in all now remaining, and as many titles. There is a table at the beginning that refers to the start of every division, where the title will also be found. But at the end of the eighth division, I find these words: *Sequitur liber 24. qui hac die etiam inceptus est, à meridie: horam circiter tertiam, per ipsum Lavanael* <note>There follows book 24, which was also begun this day, in the afternoon around three o'clock, by Lavanael himself</note>. But I find nothing following (except some blank sheets) until we come to the ninth division, *Mysteriorum pragensium, etc.* <note>The Prague Mysteries, etc.</note>. And the last division has only some fables, and before them, some five or six pages of unknown mystical words, which we do not know what to make of; but more on that later. The main business to be resolved here (as I see it) is what it is that we have and what we do not have, as far as can be gathered by what remains; we shall see what we can say about it.
