I cannot say how much (in terms of volume) that might amount to; nor will I guarantee that everything is perfect from this 28th of *May*, 1583, to the 4th of *April*, 1587, though for the most part, the coherence is sound enough up to that time. But from then until the 20th of *March*, 1607, there is a vast *chasm or hiatus* of no less than twenty years.

I cannot say for certain how this happened; my guess is this: some years after Dr. *Dee's* death ( ) Sir *Robert Cotton* bought his library (whatever remained of it then) along with his *Magical Table* (of which more later) and the *original manuscript* written in his own hand, of which this is a copy. The book had been buried in the earth; for how long—years or months—I do not know. But it was buried so long that, although it has been carefully kept since then, it retained so much of the earth that it began to mold and decay some years ago. When Sir *Thomas C.* (mentioned before) observed this, he paid to have it transcribed before it was too late. Now that nearly fifty years (or not many fewer) have passed since this original came to Sir *Robert*, it is very likely that if any more had been heard of in all that time, Sir *Robert* or his son and heir, Sir *Thomas*, would have heard of it and obtained it as soon as anyone else.

And because nothing more has been heard of for all this while, it is more than probable that no more exists, not in *England* nor, I think, anywhere else. Perhaps the rest perished—some part, if not all—even while the *Doctor* lived; and we shall find in this account *that a good part of his holy books were burned, but (what is even stranger) a great part of them were recovered and restored by the help of spirits.* Or it may be that since his death, the rest might have rotted in the earth (the place where they lay being unknown). Now, if no more exists, as is probable, we may consider what we have here to be complete in that respect, because it is everything that can be found.

But if anyone (as it is the nature of many, if not most, to desire what cannot be had rather than content themselves with what is available) should greatly lament the loss of the rest and be less pleased with this because so much is missing (though indeed we do not know for certain whether it is much or little), I would ask them to consider: in case there had been two or three times as much more as all this, what should have been done with it? For my part, regarding what is presented here (all that we had), I thought it best to have it all printed, as it is something very extraordinary and of great consequence for many good purposes and uses, even though it is somewhat long. Still, we deliberated on it, and perhaps others would have thought that less would have sufficed. # The Preface.

Very few would have thought it appropriate to have printed everything; and if it had ever come to a contraction or abridgment, much less than this might have served. Everyone is free to think as they please; for my part, all things considered, I find no great lack of the rest. And if I were forced to decide, I cannot say whether I wish more of it survived. Yet it gives me great satisfaction (and I hope there is no blasphemy or superstition in saying this, if I attribute it to providence) that after that long intermission, or *hiatus*, we still have the final actions of all. By these it might appear—after so many fine shows and promises, so much hope and expectation, so many prayers, so many thanksgivings and humiliations—what the end result is of dealing with devils and using means that are not lawful to achieve ambitious, unjustifiable desires. Besides, whether more or less is missing, I am confident we have the most important parts preserved here; specifically, an exact account of his addresses and dealings with the Emperor and other great men and princes in the seventh and some following divisions; and that tragic story of their promiscuous copulation, performed under the persuasion of obedience to God, which is related in great detail in the twelfth division. In this, the cunning and malice of evil spirits to lead people away from God (even when they most pretend to serve God and godliness) and the danger of affected uniqueness and prominence (the primary cause of all this mischief), as well as spiritual pride and self-conceit, are clearly displayed for everyone to see, provided they are not already deeply committed (as too many are in these times) to such principles.

But nevertheless, I must acknowledge that there is one part of the story missing, which I believe most readers will greatly desire. For whereas at the very beginning mention is made of a stone, and that stone is not only mentioned there but subsequently in almost every action and apparition throughout the entire book until the very end, being constantly noted and commemorated as a principal thing, it would be desirable to know what it was, how he obtained it, and indeed, what became of it, if it were possible to find out. All we are able to say of it is this: it was a stone in which, and out of which—by persons who were qualified for it and admitted to see it—all the shapes and figures mentioned in every action were seen, and voices heard. Its form was round, as appears by some rough representations of it in the margins, as on pages 395, 399 b, and 413 b; and it seems to have been of a considerable size. It seems it was most like a crystal, as it is sometimes called, such as on page 80, *Inspecto Chrystallo* <note>The crystal having been inspected</note>, and page 177 b, *nihil visibile apparuit in Chrystallo Sacrato, præter ipsius crystalli visibili formam* <note>nothing visible appeared in the consecrated crystal, except the visible form of the crystal itself</note>. Everyone knows by common experience that smooth things are best for reflections, such as mirrors and the like; but ordinarily only those things are reflected which stand opposite and are visible in their physical substance. But it is a secret of magic (which perhaps may be grounded, at least in part, upon some natural reason unknown to us) to represent objects that are not externally visible within smooth things. And Roger Bacon (also known as *Bacun*), in a manuscript titled *De dictis & factis falsorum Mathematicorum & Dæmonum* <note>On the sayings and deeds of false mathematicians and demons</note>, shared with me by my learned and much-esteemed friend Dr. *Windett*, a Professor of Medicine in *London*, has an observation to that effect in these words: *Hiis Mathematicis in malitia suâ completis apparent Dæmones sensibiliter in formâ humanâ & aliis formis variis, & dicunt & faciunt multa eis mirabilia secundum* <note>To these mathematicians, complete in their malice, demons appear tangibly in human form and other various forms, and they say and do many wonderful things for them according to...</note>

Joachim Camerarius (that worthy man mentioned before), in his preface to Plutarch’s *On Oracles, etc.*, has a strange story on the authority of a friend of his, whom he greatly respected (as he himself declares) for his piety and wisdom. A gentleman of Nuremberg had a crystal (how he obtained it can be read there) which had this quality: *If he wished to be more certain about any matter, etc.* If he desired to know anything past or future that concerned him, or indeed anyone else (in most matters), he would let a young boy (a chaste one, who was not yet of age, etc.) look into it. The boy would first see a man in it, dressed in a certain way, and afterward what he desired to know. No one but a boy so qualified could see anything in it. This crystal became very famous in those parts; indeed, some learned men came to it to be satisfied on doubtful points and had their questions answered. Yet at last (as it well deserved), it was broken into pieces by Camerarius's friend. Many such stories are to be found about magical stones and crystals. And although Fernelius, in *On the Hidden Causes of Things*, and after him (as I recall) one not inferior to Fernelius in the worth and esteem of all men—Dr. Harvey, who recently passed away—turns the account of a strange stone brought to one of the late kings of **France** into an allegory or a physical explanation of the power and properties of the element of fire; yet I am not convinced but that the account might be literally true. For it is so related by Thuanus (as I also remember here, for I have none of those books with me at this time) and understood as such by some other very learned men.

Now, as for the manner in which he obtained it, the particulars of the story cannot be found in what is preserved here, but only this in general: that it was brought to him by some whom he thought to be angels. Thus we find him telling the Emperor, *“That the angels of God had brought him a stone of such value that no earthly kingdom is worthy enough to be compared to its virtue or dignity.”* On page 272, in his conference with Dr. Curtz (who was appointed by the Emperor to negotiate with him), he says: *“and also let him see the stone brought to me by angelic ministry.”* And we find this note recorded: <note>Prague, Tuesday, September 25: I went to dinner with the Spanish Ambassador and took with me the stone brought to me by an angel, and the fourth book, in which the manner of its bringing is described.</note> And regarding the use of the stone, besides what has been said, this is noteworthy: when some spirits appeared to E. K. outside of the stone, Dr. Dee wanted the stone brought out; but E. K. said he would rather see them like this, outside the stone. # The Preface.

Some of those secrets that he claims in his books. I know some have thought him innocent, or at least have attempted to justify him. Some adopt such things to show off their wit, and think they will be considered much wiser than other men if they contradict accepted opinions, though their vanity and strong conceit of their own abilities are their chief, if not only, ground. The learned and judicious Master *Vossius* has shown himself very willing to think the best of him and his books; yet he gives up at last and rather concludes the opposite. Those who dare defend *Apollonius*—the greatest supporter of <term>Ethnicism</term> <note>Paganism or heathendom.</note> that ever lived, and considered by most heathens to be either a god or a magician—need not hesitate at anything of this kind. But regardless of what any man thinks of him (the *Trithemius* we speak of), he published his *Polygraphy* during his lifetime and dedicated it to the Emperor of that time. He tells the world of the greatest wonders to be performed by it that were ever heard of: all wisdom and arts, all languages, eloquence, and everything else were included in it. But I have never heard of any man who could make anything of it or reaped any benefit of any kind; which I think is the reason that his *Steganography*, mentioned and promised in this first work, was not printed until so long after his death. It was expected that it would have shed some light on the first work; but from neither that one nor this later one could anything be understood by any man, as far as I have ever heard. I have good ground for what I say: for besides what others have acknowledged, I find the learned *Viginaire* (who in his old age had himself become very <term>Cabalistical</term>, or perhaps had some natural disposition that way, though otherwise very learned) was as well-versed in that book as any man before him. He plainly professes he could make nothing of it. And truly, if he could not—having bestowed so much time and effort on those unprofitable studies—I see little hope that any man else should. It would make a man almost hate learning to see what foolishness even the most learned are subject to. I could bless those who know but little, provided they themselves knew that it is but little they know, and were humble. But it usually happens otherwise: those who know but little think that little to be much and are very proud of it; whereas much knowledge (or to speak properly, more knowledge), if well used, has this advantage: it makes men most sensible of their ignorance. The reading of *Viginaire’s* book of *Ciphers* (which I once thought a rare masterpiece, like many other things by the same author which I had read) has drawn these words from me in this place; and because it has such an affinity with our present theme, I was more bold. But to return: upon this consideration, I hope the reader will not be sorry that the rest of the *Tables* (being many in number) were omitted. Though I must add at the same time: had I known or thought any use could be made of them—having no better opinion of the author (him or them, I mean, from whom Dr. *Dee* received them)—I would not have been very eager to have a hand in their publication.

I should have told the reader before—but it may do well enough here—that besides the particulars previously specified, there were other things that belonged to this *holy furniture* (as Dr. *Dee* somewhere calls it), which are mentioned in some places: such as a carpet, candlestick, taper, tablecloth, cushion, and perhaps some others. However, whereas in some places he had attempted to represent the apparition, or some part of it, in figures also—this being done only occasionally, and even if it had been done more often (unless it were to satisfy the childish whim of many book buyers in this age who, because they do not buy books to read, must have something to look at; which results in much trash being accepted as good merchandise for the sake of the decorations, and vice versa), it would be of little use—no notice is taken of them, except if some figure is in the text itself and is of some consequence for a better understanding of the rest.

The Greek on page 25b is set out exactly as it was found, and as it can still be seen in the original, written by Dr. Dee himself. But little or nothing can be made of it as it is written; and it is a sign that Dr. Dee—who wrote it down as *Edward Kelley* reported it to him and afterwards puzzled over it (as appears by some conjectures and interpretations found in the original and presented here as well) as best he could—was not a very perfect Greek scholar; much less *Edward Kelley*, who could not even read it. This led Dr. Dee to write some things that he did not want Kelley to read in Greek characters, even though the words were English. I would not alter anything that was in the original. But the words, which I believe were spoken by the spirit (and thus the Greek is justifiable enough), were these: Οὗτος ὁ ἑταῖρος τοῦτο ἔργον ἀναστήσει : Κόσμος γὰρ πρόθυμος τυγχάνει ὤν : Κὶ αὐτὸς τοσοῦτον πειράζεται : Ἥστε κοινῆς ἀφελκύσθαι φιλίας : Ἐσόρα μὴ τινὰ αὐτῷ ἀφορμὴν παρέχῃς : Τὰς γδ̈ <note>abbreviation for γὰρ</note> ἁπάλας κομιδῇ παρασκευάζεται : Ἵνα σε διὰ παντὸς ἀπολείπῃ. This, I think, was intended to refer to *Edward Kelley*, who was constantly planning to break with Dr. Dee and leave, as occurs shortly after here and in various other places in this account; indeed, he did actually forsake him at times for a while. The literal sense is this: *This fellow (or friend) will overthrow this work* (of apparitions, you must understand, for which he was necessary, because the Devil did not have the power over Dr. Dee's body to prepare it for such visions, though he promised it to him). *His baggage (or equipment) is ready. And he strives very hard to withdraw himself from this mutual friendship. Take heed that you give him no reason; for he plots mightily by art and cunning how he may leave you forever.* Πρόθυμος, in the first line, may seem unusual instead of ἕτοιμος or πρόθυρος; but it is an elegant metaphor. Πειράζεται for πειρᾶται is not usual; and perhaps it should have been πειρᾶται, and spoken as such; but that is of no importance. Certainly, he who could speak so much Greek (called "Syrian" here to mock Edward Kelley) could not lack Latin at any time to express himself.

I cannot think of anything else of this nature that the reader needs to be told, and perhaps some of this might have been spared. However, the reader should consider that, as in all books, so in this: it is one thing to read from the beginning and proceed with care and observation without skipping, and another thing to read here and there. This would require a constant commentary, which is the misfortune of most readers in these declining days of learning; and therefore they have comments (or rather, rhapsodies) accordingly; *similes habent labra lactucas*, never was anything more true.

Perhaps some will wonder what caused the *spirits* to discuss *English* genealogies and histories; this occurs at the very beginning, so I mention it for the sake of the reader who is still (and cannot be otherwise) a stranger to the book. The matter is that Dr. *Dee* had recently entered into a great alliance and confederacy with *Albert Lasky* (or *à Lasco* rather), a great man of *Poland*. You have heard before what *Camden* says of him regarding his coming to *England* at this very time and his departure, which agrees very well with our dates here. It seems that, although he was nobly born and held great dignity, his thoughts aspired much higher; and though he was not a rich man for someone of his rank and quality, because he expected such things from Dr. *Dee* and his *spirits* as he did, he could find enough money to supply their needs when necessary. The spirits were very glad of the opportunity and did what they could to encourage him according to his temperament. Being then at that very time engaged in deliberations that depended much on *Albert Lasky* and his good opinion, among other things, his pedigree—which must certainly please a vain man very well—was taken into consideration. I do not guarantee that everything said there exactly matches the truth, nor am I at leisure at this time to take the trouble to examine it. We must never look further into things delivered by such beings than to see if they were or are pertinent (whether true or false) to their purpose and the current occasion. Besides, it is very possible (which I desire the reader to take good notice of) that both here and elsewhere the transcribers, because they sometimes could not read the text and were forced to leave some blanks (though seldom to any considerable harm to the sense), might also have made mistakes, dealing as they were with an original that was (and still can be seen) as defaced and worm-eaten as this is, written (as we have said) by Dr. *Dee* himself.

Besides the authenticity of the original copy, written by Dr. *Dee* himself, the reader should know that the originals of the *letters* presented here are all, or most of them, still preserved and can be seen in Sir *Thomas Cotton's* library.

IV. I have now come to the last of the four things I promised: to show the various good uses that may be made of this book, which were the main reasons for publishing it. I indeed proposed this order to myself, but since a great part of this topic presented itself during other matters, it has already been covered in the previous discourse, so that little is now left to be done. However, I will sum them up and present them together, so that every reader may have

...to have them in readiness and in view for his use all the better.

The first point is against Atheists, and those who do not believe that there are any Devils or Spirits: We have argued this, I confess, quite extensively at the beginning of this Discourse or Preface, and I hope some may receive sufficient satisfaction from what we have stated. But if no argument had been used (setting aside Scripture Authority, which would be irrelevant against Atheists), I do not know what could be more convincing than this distressing story, so exactly, so particularly, and so faithfully delivered. Truly, they must see further than I do who can find anything to answer (rationally) or to oppose. This is a great point and a major foundation of Religion; but this is not all. For if there are spirits indeed—so wicked and malicious, so diligent and so industrious in deluding men and doing mischief, which is their goal, all of which is so fully represented in this account—then it must certainly follow that there is a great overruling Power that takes care of the Earth and its inhabitants; especially those who adore that Power and worship it with true affection and sincerity. For without this overruling Power, what a miserable world would we have? What man could be so sober or innocent that he could enjoy himself at any time with any comfort or security? But again, what man can read this distressing story and be so convinced of his own wisdom or innocence that he will not, in some degree, reflect upon himself? And he will be moved to praise God that, despite many provocations of various kinds (such as damnable curiosity, open profaneness, frequent oaths, curses, perjuries, a scandalous life, and the like), God has been pleased to protect and preserve him from the force and violence of such enemies of mankind?

I said before that the greatest confusions have followed from small beginnings, which is very true, as in the case of *Bacchus* particularly many ages ago, and in the case of *Mahomet* afterwards (two notable, wicked enthusiasts through whom, as instruments, evil *spirits*—by God's permission—brought great alterations to governments and wrought much mischief and villainy among men and women), as we shall show more at length elsewhere. By due consideration of all circumstances—chiefly their confident and repeated addresses to, and attempts upon, so many great men in power and authority, and the like—I am strongly of the opinion that these spirits had as great hopes for Dr. *Dee* as they ever had for *Bacchus* or *Mahomet*. But God was not pleased at that time to permit their malice and subtlety to prevail. And I think, if we consider it well, we have reason to praise God for it. *England* might have been overrun with *Anabaptism* (when I say *Anabaptism*, I mean *Anabaptism* confirmed and in full power, not as it appears in its first pretensions) long before this. God be thanked that it was not then, and God keep it from it still; I hope this is the prayer of all truly sober and religious people. And indeed, I know no reason why the wisdom and prudence of their Majesties' Council at that time, in opposing Dr. *Dee's* frequent addresses and solicitations, may not (under God) claim and deserve some part of our thanks and acknowledgement.

Again, we see the Devil can pray and preach (in outward appearance, we mean; for truly and really, God forbid that anything sacred and holy should be thought to proceed from devils) and talk of sanctity and mortification as well as the best. And what he can do in his own person, or by himself immediately—

...diately; there is no question that he does so through his ministers and instruments much more—more ordinarily and frequently, I mean. Let any man judge then, whether it is the part of a sober, wise man not only to listen to such men as can give no account of their calling, but also to follow them, to embrace their *Doctrine*, and to be of their number or congregation—and all this for the reason that they can pray and preach very well (at least as they think and judge) and talk very godlily and zealously? How much more inexcusable are those who will cling to such men, even though they see and know them to be scandalous in their lives—proud, insolent, ignorant, seditious, and intolerable—simply because they can pray, preach, and talk in a way that best agrees with their own humor and gives them the most satisfaction? Can anyone think they follow God in this, who would have *all things done in order* and is not a *God of confusion* (1 Cor. 14:33, 40), when everything they do tends toward nothing but disorder and confusion? I confess it is possible that men who are lawfully called may prove bad enough; we have various examples in the Scripture. But if a man is simply and ignorantly misled by such people, certainly his judgment will be much lighter than what can be expected by those who will not use the means that God has ordained in so great and weighty a business as the salvation of souls is. I do not know what these men can say for themselves, unless it is that they are resolved to make use of the liberty of the times to please their humor; they may do so, but if that brings them to heaven, they have good luck indeed.

But the matter of praying is what I would principally insist upon. You see here how Dr. *Dee*, where he gives an account of himself to the Emperor and others, relies heavily on this: that for so many years he had been an earnest suitor to God through *prayer* to obtain *wisdom*—such wisdom as he was ambitious for. I believe him, that he had prayed very earnestly and with much importunity many times. This was what made him so confident about his spirits—that they must necessarily be good spirits and angels. I know a man—it gives me no comfort to tell it, except that I would not conceal anything that may serve as a warning to others, and yet I will still show respect to him too—but I knew one, a very innocent man (in his outward conversation, and as I believe, very much so in reality): humble, religious, very learned and orthodox, and one who had suffered for his conscience as others have done in these times. This worthy man, being engaged in a controversial argument upon which his fancy had worked very much—or rather, which had worked much upon his fancy—had written a great deal, filled much paper, and was desirous to communicate to me as his friend what he had done. But when I perceived that the drift of his writing was from the Law and the Prophets, to show the necessity of some things which I thought were of a more indifferent nature, I was not willing to meddle with it, and began to argue against his main point and to show my dislike of it. After many words back and forth, he began to press me with this: that he had often prayed with much earnestness, and he was very confident that God had heard his prayers. Indeed, he went so far as to say that if God were true, he could not be deceived, and used many other words to the same purpose, at which I was much amazed, but could

...could do him no good, such was his confidence and violence on this occasion, though he was otherwise a very moderate and honest man. And so I found him more than once or twice. Truly, I think God was very merciful to him by taking him away in good time. But certainly this business of *Prayer* and *praising* is a business of great comfort (the greatest that mortal man is capable of on earth), yet also of much more danger and delusion than many believe. And if caution and circumspection are to be used in anything belonging to Religion, I think they ought to be used in Prayer as much as anything. And since I have ventured to tell one story on my own credit, I will tell one more on better authority, which I have long desired (because it is so noteworthy) to communicate to the world; and to that end, I once inserted it in a treatise of mine, which I thought would have been printed, but it was not. I will first give the English translation of it, so that everyone may benefit, and then set it down in the words of my author (my own father *Isaac Casaubon*, of <note>blessed memory</note>) as I have it shown in his own hand.

*At a Consistory in Geneva, on Friday, July 18, 1589: The case of one Mr. Nicholas was proposed to the Assembly for consideration; he was accustomed to insinuate himself into various houses under the pretense of praying, and he formed small congregations. The business was disliked by the Pastors: First, because nothing in the Church of God ought to be done without order. Secondly, because it was not lawful to turn such duties of Religion into a matter of trade to get money only (without any other purpose or calling). Thirdly and lastly, his <term>battalogy</term> (or vain repetition of words) was not to be tolerated. Then on this occasion, Mr. Beza related that on the Saturday before, while that sharp conflict was occurring which we had before our eyes (namely, between the Genevans and the Duke of Savoy's forces), a certain woman addressed him, saying, "What, Mr. Beza, will you say prayers here?" To which he had answered, "No." "What, do you think I behold these things with my eyes only, and do not pray to God in my heart?" Giving this reason for the answer he had made to the woman:* <note>It is not expressed this way in the Latin—that the following words were Beza’s words—but the coherence of the matter requires it.</note> *That Prayer was certainly a holy thing, which it did not become any man to apply himself to (or to undertake) without due preparation. And that those who thought it was such an easy thing to pray correctly were deceived. And that care should also be taken lest <note>under the pretense of zeal and devotion</note> a way be opened for superstition. The Latin words are these:*

[Die Veneris, Julii 18. 1589. Cùm relatum esset in cœtum, de Mag. Nicolao, qui insinuaret se in domos varias προφάσει τοῦ εὔχεσθαι, & ita aliquando cœtus, etsi paruos, coire solitos, pastoribus res improbata est: Primùm, quia extra ordinem, nihil in Dei Ecclesia fieri debet: Deinde, quia πορισμὸν facere τὴν θρησκείαν, nefas. Tertio, hominis βαττολογία non ferenda Narratum est tum à B se die Sabbathi proxime præcedente, dum acerrimum illud prælium committeretur, quod nobis erat ante oculos, interrogatum à muliercula, *Quid tu D. B. vis preces hic facere?* Respondisse, *Nequaquam. Tu ne enim (ait) me putas, hæc oculis tantum spectare, nec vota in animo ad Deum Opt. Max. fundere? Omnino,*]

*res sancta ἡ εὐχὴ, ad quam non nisi meditatum oporteat accedere, falluntur enim qui rem putant esse facilem, preces benè concipere. Simul cavendum, ne alicui superstitioni viam imprudentes aperiamus.]*

Finally, all men may take warning from this example of how they remove themselves from the protection of Almighty God, either through presumptuous, unlawful wishes and desires, or by seeking help not only from devils directly (which Dr. Dee certainly never did, but rather abhorred the very thought of it in his heart) but from those who are most closely related to devils, such as *witches, wizards, conjurers, astrologers* (who take it upon themselves to foretell human events), *fortune-tellers*, and the like—yes, and all books on that subject, which I suspect were a major cause of Dr. Dee's delusion. It is certain enough that people are commonly cheated by such individuals; and those who are not complete fools would be careful how they deal with them and would avoid them to escape the reputation of being fools. But those who are wise would avoid them even more if they can do more than merely cheat; for the more they are capable of doing, the more they know they have the devil in them. Wretched people! They will not and dare not trust God, who, as He is the only fountain of goodness, also alone knows what is good for every person. They may rejoice for a time and applaud themselves for their imagined successes, but misery will be their end if they do not repent; and it is a great sign that God is very angry with them when He allows them to thrive by means that He Himself has cursed.

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, transitioning into a postscript that addresses Elias Ashmole’s recently published account of Dr. Dee and Edward Kelley, while providing a contrasting, more critical view of Kelley’s character and actions.</meta>

# POSTSCRIPT.

Since this Preface was written and almost printed, I was shown a book titled *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum*, etc., by *Elias Ashmole, Esq.*; and in some *annotations* there at the end, an account concerning Dr. *Dee* and *Edward Kelley* (there styled Sir *Edward Kelley*), taken from a *diary* of Dr. *Dee’s*, all written in his own hand. Just as I do not question the gentleman’s honesty in this matter, I also have little doubt that Dr. *Dee’s* own handwriting will be found to agree on all matters of fact both here and there, if anyone takes the trouble to compare them. And perhaps the reader may find some further satisfaction in certain details through his work, which is the reason I mention the book here, having only recently learned of it. I do not interfere with his judgment regarding either Dr. *Dee* or *Kelley*; and perhaps, had he seen what is presented here, he would have held a different opinion on some matters. There is enough here, I am certain, to satisfy any man who is not already biased or otherwise motivated by personal interests.

As for those *reports* concerning *Kelley* (some of which also involve Dr. *Dee*) that he mentions, while I believe him that he has heard such things, I must (and may truly) declare that I have encountered very different reports, which, in my judgment and according to this account given to us by Dr. *Dee*, are much more probable. Specifically, I have heard that *Kelley* was imprisoned by the Emperor for a notable chemical fraud he had committed against him; although the details were fully related to me, I will not venture to repeat them, lest I make a mistake in some technical terms or minor circumstances of the facts.

And let the reader judge by the account Dr. *Dee* (who knew him best) provides throughout this entire book about this *Kelley*, whether *Weever’s* story in his *Funeral Monuments, pages 45, 46*—of damnable <term>necromancy</term> and other *diabolical conjuration* practiced by *Kelley* in *Lancashire*—is not (in addition to what is stated and attested there) much more probable than anything that has been or can be said by others in his defense or praise. This indeed makes Doctor *Dee’s* case completely inexcusable: that, believing and knowing the man to be such a person, he would still associate with him and expect good results from his services. But the Doctor’s faith and his intellect (by God’s just judgment, as we have said) were so much under the power and control of his spirits that they could persuade him to do anything under the guise of serving God—yes, even if it had been to cut his own father’s throat. As we see in the *Relation*, they persuaded him to lie with another man’s wife and prostitute his own to a man he himself believed to be vile and diabolical.

Additionally, I have been told by many that Dr. *Dee*, very poor and miserable in every way, died at *Mortlake* near *London*, which does not seem to agree with the report in those *annotations*. But enough of those. I have not said anything at all for the purpose of opposing the author, but rather to provide further satisfaction to the reader, or rather to the truth, which I felt I was bound to do.

The passage in *Weever’s Funeral Monuments, pages 45, 46* regarding *Kelley*, for the satisfaction of those who do not have the book, is this: *Kelley* (otherwise called *Talbot*), that famous *English* alchemist of our times, who, after fleeing his own country (having lost both his ears at *Lancaster*), was entertained by *Rudolf* the Second—the last Emperor of *Germany* of that Christian name. Queen *Elizabeth* of famous memory sent (very secretly) Captain *Peter Gwyn* with some others to persuade him to return to his native home, which he was willing to do. However, while attempting to escape by stealth at night by climbing over a wall of his own house in *Prague* (which bears his name to this day and was once an old sanctuary), he fell from the battlements, broke his legs, and bruised his body. He died from these injuries shortly thereafter.

*But to what purpose is this?* you will ask. Then consider this: this diabolical questioning of the dead to gain knowledge of future events was practiced by the said *Kelley*. One night, in the park of *Walton-le-Dale* in the County of *Lancaster*, he and one *Paul Waring* (his companion in such deeds of darkness) summoned someone from the infernal ranks to learn certain details of the life, as well as what might be known through the devil’s foresight, regarding the manner and time of the death of a noble young gentleman who was then in <term>wardship</term>.

When the black ceremonies of that night were finished, *Kelley* asked one of the gentleman’s servants which corpse was the last to be buried in *Low Churchyard* (a church adjoining the park). The servant told him of a poor man who had been buried there that same day. He and the said *Waring* urged this servant to go with them to the grave of the man so recently interred, which he did; and he also helped them dig up the corpse of the poor wretch. By their incantations, they made him (or rather some evil spirit through his vocal organs) speak, and he delivered strange predictions concerning the said gentleman. I was told this much by the said servant, who was a secondary participant in that dismal and abhorred business; and several gentlemen and others are still living in *Lancashire* to whom he has related this story. And the gentleman himself (whose memory I am bound to honor) told me shortly before his death about this conjuration by *Kelley*, as he had heard it from his servant and tenant, with only a few circumstances excepted that the servant thought inappropriate to share with his master.

# Dr. Dee's Apology,

## Sent to the Archbishop of CANTERBURY. 1594/5.

->OR,<-

# A Letter containing a very brief Apologetic Discourse, with a plain demonstration and fervent protestation for the lawful, sincere, very faithful, and Christian course of the Philosophical Studies and Exercises of a certain studious gentleman: An ancient servant to Her most Excellent Royal Majesty.

->**To the most Reverend Father in God, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate and Metropolitan of all England, one of Her Majesty’s most Honorable Privy Council: my singularly good Lord.**<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'M' featuring two human figures (possibly cherubs) and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

Most humbly and heartily I crave your Grace's pardon if I cause any offense by sending or presenting to your Grace's hand so simple a discourse as this is. Although, in the opinion of some of my wise and discreet friends, it is thought not to be irrelevant to my most necessary petitions currently being handled (before her most Excellent Royal Majesty, your Lordship's good Grace, and other the Right Honorable Lords of her Majesty’s Privy Council) to first make known and reveal to your Grace and other the Right Honorable, my good Lords of her Majesty’s Privy Council, some part of my former studies and scholarly exercises (practiced and continued for these past 46 years). And secondly, afterward, to permit the same to be published: not so much to stop the mouths and finally halt the impudent attempts of the rash and malicious schemers and inventors of most untrue, foolish, and wicked reports and fables regarding my aforementioned scholarly exercises—conducted with my great (indeed incredible) pains, labors, cares, and costs in the search for and learning of true philosophy—but rather, in doing so, to certify and satisfy the godly and impartial Christian listener or reader of this. That, by his own judgment (upon his due consideration and examination of this substantial portion of the details of my aforementioned studies and philosophical exercises attached here), he will or may be sufficiently informed and persuaded that I have labored wonderfully to find, follow, use, and frequent the true, straight, and most narrow path leading all true, devout, zealous, faithful, and constant Christians...

<header>APOLOGETICAL.</header>
<sig>K</sig>
<meta>catchword: 4. The</meta>

Christian students, *from this valley of misery, and from the misery of that valley; and from the Kingdom of darkness, and from the darkness of that Kingdom, to the holy mount Zion and to the heavenly tabernacles.* All thanks are most due, therefore, to the Almighty. Since it so pleased him (even from my youth, by his divine favor, grace, and help) to instill into my heart an insatiable zeal and desire to know his truth: and in him, and by him, incessantly to seek and listen for the same, by the true philosophical method and harmony: proceeding and ascending (as it were) *gradatim* <note>step by step</note>, from things visible to consider things invisible; from things bodily to conceive of things spiritual; from things transitory and momentary to meditate on things permanent; and by things mortal (visible and invisible) to have some perception <note>The original uses "perseverance," which in this context means discernment or perception.</note> of immortality. And to conclude most briefly: by the most marvelous frame of the whole world—philosophically viewed and circumspectly weighed, numbered, and measured (according to the talent and gift of God allotted from above for the effecting of his divine purposes)—to most faithfully love, honor, and glorify always the Framer and Creator of it. In whose workmanship his infinite goodness, unsearchable wisdom, and Almighty power—yes, his everlasting power and divinity—may (by innumerable means) be manifested and demonstrated. The truth of my zealous, careful, and constant intent and endeavor as specified may (I hope) easily appear by the whole, full, and due survey and consideration of all the books, treatises, and discourses whose titles only are, at this time, here annexed and expressed. These are set down in the sixth chapter of another little rhapsodical treatise entitled *The Compendious Rehearsal, etc.*, written over two years ago for those two honorable Commissioners of her Majesty, whom her most Excellent Majesty had most graciously sent to my poor cottage in Mortlake to understand the matters and causes in full. Because of these, I was so extremely urged to procure from her Majesty's hands such honorable surveyors and witnesses to be assigned for the due proof of the contents of my most humble and pitiful supplication, exhibited to her most Excellent Majesty at Hampton Court on November 9, 1592. Thus, therefore (as follows), is the said 6th chapter recorded there.

> ¶ *My labors and pains bestowed at various times to please my native country: by the writing of various books and treatises; some in Latin, some in English, and some of them written at her Majesty’s command.*

Of which books and treatises, some are printed and some unprinted. The printed books and treatises are these following:

1. **P**ropædeumata Aphoristica, *On certain more outstanding virtues of Nature. 120 Aphorisms.* Year 1558.

2. *Monas Hieroglyphica, mathematically and anagogically explained;* to Maximilian (by the grace of God) the most wise King of the Romans, Bohemia, and Hungary. Year 1564.

3. *Letter to the eminent mathematician of the Duke of Urbino* (Federico Commandino) *prefixed to the book of Mohammed of Baghdad, "On the Divisions of Surfaces"; published by my labor and that of the same Commandino of Urbino; printed at Pesaro.* Year 1570.

* In that library, there were about 4,000 books, of which 700 were ancient manuscripts. Some were in Greek, some in Latin, some in *Hebrew*, and some in other languages (as may appear by the full *Catalogus* <note>Catalog</note> of them). But the great losses and damages I have suffered in various ways do not grieve my heart as much as the rash, wicked, foolish, and most untrue fables and reports about me and my philosophical studies have done and still do. Commonly, after their first hatching and devilish invention, these are immediately spread with great speed across the whole realm. To some they seem true; to others they are doubtful; and only to the wise, modest, discreet, godly, and charitable (and especially to those who have some acquaintance with me) do they appear and are known to be fables, untruths, and utterly false reports and slanders. Well, this shall be my last charitable warning and fervent protestation to my countrymen and all others in this case;

# A fervent PROTESTATION.

*Before the Almighty our* GOD, *and your Lordship’s good Grace, this day, on the peril of my soul’s damnation (if I lie or take His name in vain herein), I take the same* GOD *to be my witness; That with all my heart, with all my soul, with all my strength, power, and understanding (according to the measure of it which the Almighty has given me), for the most part of the time from my youth until now, I have used and still use good, lawful, honest, Christian, and divinely prescribed means to attain the knowledge of those truths which are appropriate and necessary for me to know; and with which to do His divine Majesty such service as He has, does, and will call me to during this my life: for the advancement of His honor and glory, and for the benefit and public advantage of this Kingdom; as much as, by the will and purpose of God, shall lie in my skill and ability to perform: as a true, faithful, and most sincerely dutiful servant to our most gracious and incomparable* Queen Elizabeth, *and as a very comfortable fellow-member of the body politic, governed under the Royal scepter of our earthly Supreme head (* Queen Elizabeth *), and as a lively, sympathetic, and true symmetrical fellow-member of that holy and mystical body, universally <note>In the original: Catholiquely</note> extended and placed (wherever) on the earth: in the view, knowledge, direction, protection, illumination, and consolation of the Almighty, most Blessed, most holy, most glorious, co-majestic, co-eternal, and co-essential Trinity: The Head of that Body being only our Redeemer,* Christ Jesus, *perfect God and perfect man: whose return in glory we faithfully await, and daily do very earnestly cry to Him to hasten His second coming for His elect’s sake; iniquity does so abound and prevail on this earth, and true faith with Charity and Evangelical simplicity have but cold, slender, and uncertain reception among the worldly-wise men of this world.*

*Therefore (concluding here), I beseech the Almighty God most abundantly to increase and confirm your Grace’s heavenly wisdom, and endow you with all the rest of His heavenly gifts, for the relieving, refreshing, and comforting, both bodily and spiritually, His little flock of the faithful, yet militant here on earth.*
->Amen.<-

---

## An EPILOGUE.

My good Lord, I beseech Your Grace to allow my plain and comfortable *Epilogus* <note>Epilogue</note> for this matter at this time. 1. Seeing that my studious exercises and civil conversation may be abundantly testified to my good credit in most parts of all *Christendom*; and that by all degrees of Nobility, by all degrees of the Learned, and by very many others of godly and Christian disposition, through the trial of forty-six years: (as appears by the Records lately viewed by two honorable witnesses, by Commission from her Majesty;) 2. And seeing that, for these last thirty-six years, I have been her most Excellent Majesty’s very true, faithful, and dutiful servant; from whose Royal mouth I never received a single word of reproach, but only favor and grace: In whose Princely Countenance I never perceived a frown toward me, or a look of discontent or view of

me; but at all times favorable and gracious, to the great joy and comfort of my true, faithful, and loyal heart. And (thirdly), seeing that the works of my hands and words of my mouth (previously noted here in the schedule of my books and writings) may bear living witness to the thoughts of my heart and the inclination of my mind generally (as all wise men know, and Christ himself avouches), it might in a way seem needless to have so carefully (though most briefly and quickly) warned or confounded the scornful, the malicious, the proud, and the rash in their untrue reports, opinions, and fables of my philosophical studies or exercises. However, it is of more importance that the godly, the honest, the modest, the discreet, grave, and charitable Christians (English or otherwise), lovers of justice, truth, and good learning, may hereby receive certain comfort in themselves (to perceive that *Veritas tandem prævalebit* <note>Truth will at last prevail</note>) and be sufficiently weaponed and armed with sound truth to defend me against such adversaries, should they hereafter begin afresh or obstinately hold on to their former errors, vain imaginations, false reports, and most ungodly slanders of me and my studies.

¶ Therefore (to put this matter beyond all doubt forever before God and man), seeing that your Lordship's good grace is, as it were, our high priest and chief ecclesiastical minister (under our most revered and sovereign Lady Queen Elizabeth), to whose censure and judgment I submit all my studies and exercises—yes, all my books past, present, and hereafter to be written by me (of my own skill, judgment, or opinion)—I do at this present time most humbly, sincerely, and unfeignedly, and in the name of Almighty God (yes, for His honor and glory), request and beseech your Grace (when and as conveniently as you may) to be well and thoroughly informed of what I am, *Intus & in cute* <note>Inside and out; literally, "Within and under the skin"</note>: *Reverendissime in Christo Pater, & Dignissime Archipræsul, cognosce & agnosce vultum tàm internum, quàm externum pecoris tui* <note>Most Reverend Father in Christ and most worthy Archbishop, know and recognize both the internal and external face of your flock</note>. And if I have used, do use, or shall use pen, speech, or conversation in any way other than what pertains to a faithful, careful, sincere, and humble servant of Christ Jesus, I ask that your Grace would deign to advise me. So, I trust, *Ultima respondebunt primis* <note>The end will match the beginning</note>, in such a way as this authentic record annexed in Latin (*ad perpetuam rei memoriam* <note>for the perpetual memory of the matter</note>) testifies. I have never until now had occasion to show that in any place in Christendom to testify better of me than they had proof of me themselves through my conduct among them. (The Almighty, therefore, be highly thanked, praised, honored, and glorified, forever and ever, Amen.)

But now, regarding the general intent of this brief discourse, I most humbly and reverently present for your Grace's view and reading the original document and authentic record mentioned before, clearly written on parchment, with the seal whole and perfect, duly attached, as I have preserved it for forty-six years and somewhat longer. The true copy of it, as your Grace sees, follows word for word.

# A LETTER

To all the children of the Holy Mother Church to whom these present letters shall come, the Vice-Chancellor and the whole assembly of Regents and non-Regents of the University of Cambridge send eternal greeting in the Lord. Sincerely considering the conditions and merits of those studying in our University, we judge that those alone should be honored with our testimony whom we know, because of their learning and integrity of character, to have deserved this benefit from us. Therefore, since at this time truth itself demands our testimony, we signify to your piety by these letters that our beloved in Christ, **John Dee**, Master of Arts, having successfully conducted himself in our said University, has gained for himself great praise for both learning and honesty. Lest any ambiguity or question might arise anywhere regarding his degree and conduct (which was always most honorable) among those to whom this man's virtues are not sufficiently known, it has seemed good to us to write these our testimonial letters for the benefit of the said **John**, and having written them, to seal them with the public seal of our Academy; so that our letters may have greater authority and weight among you. Fare well. Given at Cambridge, in full Convocation of the Masters Regent and non-Regent of the aforesaid Academy: March 19 [the 14th day before the Calends of April], in the year since Christ’s birth, **1548.**

->For certain appropriate reasons, the exact image of the aforementioned seal is not published here in portraiture; the motto: *The place of the true seal.*<-

---

## PERORATIO.

> The Almighty and most merciful God, the Father; for the sake of his only Son (our Redeemer) Jesus Christ: by his holy Spirit, so direct, bless, and prosper all my studies and philosophical exercises (yes, all my thoughts, words, and deeds) from now on, even to the very moment of my departing from this world, that I may clearly and abundantly be found, and undoubtedly acknowledged by the wise and just, to have been a zealous and faithful student in the school of truth, and an ancient graduate in the school of charity: to the honor and glory of the same God Almighty, and to the sound comfort and confirming of such as faithfully love and fear his Divine Majesty, and unfeignedly continue in labor to do good on earth: when, while, to whom, and as they may, *Amen.*

->Very quickly written, this twelfth evening and twelfth day, in my poor cottage at Mortlake: In the year 1595, current from the birth of Christ; but in the year 1594 complete from his conception, with nine additional months completed.<-

->*Always, and very dutifully, at your Grace’s command:*<-

**Jo. Dee.**

I. Page 1.
The first apparition of *Madimi*, in the shape of a girl. *Alb. Lasky*, his pedigree. This *Al. L.* (of whom there is more in the Preface) being the first designed by the Spirits as a fit instrument, under the pretense of godliness and reformation, to turn all things upside down in the world: But that plot failing, then the Emperor of *Germany*; after him *Stephen*, King of *Poland*; after him, Prince *Rosimberg*, were considered, and applications (as will be found here) were made to them for that purpose. What changes and destructions of men and kingdoms would have followed (had God permitted it, as in *Mahomet's* case, etc.) may be gathered from various passages in this book.

III p. 5. Mystical numbers and letters for a magical lamin. <note>A lamin or lamina is a thin plate of metal or other material used in magic rituals.</note>

¶ p. 244. Doctor Dee is comforted and confirmed by his spirits against slanders and evil reports, using Scripture, etc. The spirits here seem to allude to a passage in the Sibylline Oracles (a counterfeit book), as Doctor Dee eventually observes its agreement with them. They tell Doctor Dee he shall be with the Emperor in spite of the Devil (for they can mock themselves when they wish, to fool men); but they did not speak the truth, and in that they showed themselves to be true devils. Doctor Dee might have understood this, had his understanding not been so blinded and captivated by them.

¶ Doctor Dee is invited to dinner by the Spanish Ambassador, who, among other things, claims to be descended from Raymundus Lullius. He claims that this Raymundus Lullius (if we may believe him), through retired solitude without books (a method also commended recently, but indeed the quickest way to drive men out of their wits), changed from an ignorant, illiterate man to a very learned one, and that he possessed the Philosopher’s Stone. Based on this, he concludes and maintains that what Doctor Dee related about himself—his visions and revelations, etc.—might be just as possible and true. The Emperor is commended by him.

The doctrine of transubstantiation: of receiving under one kind: of adoration of the Eucharist; but receiving it was not allowed.*

->Part II.<-

Action I. p. 1. *Sermon-like material*: *Doctor Dee* (having a zeal, but not according to knowledge) is marvelously affected by it. *Prince Rosenberg’s* expectation of money is answered and eluded with great subtlety, by examples from Scripture—of *Abraham, David, Solomon, etc.* The precious Powder he had: how and when it was to be used. *Judgments* to be executed upon several Great ones (certainly enough if they had prevailed) by *Prince Rosenberg*, as if from God. *Edward Kelley’s* wife is barren: why. He is very weary of his office: reproved for it, and another (*Arthur, Doctor Dee’s son*) to be substituted in his place; indeed, his portion of the precious Powder is to be taken from him if he does not repent.
II. p. 4. *Arthur*, first presented and prepared by prayer, *etc.*, enters upon his office: sees diverse things in the Stone; lions, men, *etc.*, but hears nothing.
III. p. 5. *Arthur* again, as before: three exercises in one day.
IV. p. 7. *Arthur* again, as before: in two more exercises.
V. p. 8. *Edward Kelley* in his office again: sees and hears as before. *Uriel*, the first author of *Doctor Dee’s* and *Edward Kelley’s* conjunction. A New Law is promised here again. *Anabaptist doctrine of committing adultery for God's sake, etc.*
<margin>¶ For some words here, see the Errata.</margin>
VI. P. 9. Here the spirits begin to show themselves in their own likeness apparently, teaching doctrines of devils—and yet still (as their instruments at this day in diverse places) in the name of God. *Doctor Dee* and *Edward Kelley* are exhorted, indeed commanded, to have their wives in common. The case is argued on both sides stiffly and eagerly. Other strange doctrine of devils (noted and rejected in the Preface) of murder, condemned by the laws of men, yet approved by God. *Saint Paul* is impiously slandered. Great promises in case of obedience. The Powder. The Pope here 

<column-break/>

accursed: yet *Popery* elsewhere justified. *Kelley* scandalized; *Doctor Dee* in great agony. Some secrets of distillation revealed by spirits. The Powder again, and how *E. K.* obtained it. Predictions regarding *England, etc.* (all false and foolish). *Edward Kelley’s* fidelity suspected. Cabalistic mysteries of letters and numbers: not well understood by *Doctor Dee, etc.*, though much helped by his spirits. But at last, he has joy (in spirit, as he is persuaded) and resolves to obey.
¶ *Doctor Dee, Edward Kelley*, and their two wives: their sense, apprehensions, and resolutions concerning this newly enjoined doctrine of promiscuous copulation; expressed in the form of a Covenant (so called by them) with God: here first exhibited, and afterwards, p. 20, completed and subscribed by the parties: ¶ with a most wicked clause, or conclusion, of dreadful imprecations to all who should hereafter come to the knowledge of it, or bring it to light; whereas it is much to the glory of God and true religion that such mysteries of Hell and darkness should come to light to be abhorred by all men, and so that others may be warned by such sad examples not to hunt after new doctrines and pretended inspirations and revelations.
¶ P. 17. *Edward Kelley’s* declaration of his dislike, from the beginning of these actions in general: his opposition upon occasion. His dislike of this new doctrine (in particular) as contrary to the revealed Will of God: how he was satisfied in some measure, and thereupon his readiness to obey. But upon the women's professed dislike and demurs, he resolves to give up all further dealing.
VII, p. 19. *Apparitions*. The chief Stone carried away by spirits in their sight. More exhortations and arguments for compliance with this new doctrine. Offer of a miracle for further confirmation.
VIII, p. 21. Another *apparition* (upon request made) to confirm them in their purpose of obedience.
IX, p. 22. Yet another to the same purpose. The *Covenant* torn by *Kelley*, made whole again by spirits. The great power of God: faith and obedience.

<column-break/>

and probably with his life: or at least (though his spirits had promised him, p. 34, the addition of many years) not long before his death. I cannot yet learn the exact time of his death: but it was much about this time (according to all reports) and in England, certainly. Although his sin was very great (as shown in the Preface), yet because of his simple and sincere intentions toward God, it may charitably be hoped that God was so merciful to him as to let him know his error and to repent of it before his death.
¶ p. 46. That which follows here is certainly intended to be part of that **holy Language** which **Adam** in Paradise is said (Part 1, p. 64, 92) to have spoken, and by which great wonders might be performed. I have neither the faith nor the curiosity to inquire into it any further; nor, I think, will any sober man.

---

Instead of other approval, the reader (besides the judgment of the late **Archbishop of Armagh**—so famous everywhere for his piety and learning; mentioned in the first page of the Preface—and the judgment of various others who read the manuscript book and wished it printed) may consider how solicitous the Devil has been when he saw his plots (God opposing them) not likely to take effect, so that these **Mysteries** (these papers and records) might not come to light. First, by p. 418 and p. 431 (**Doctor Dee’s** letter to the **Pope's Nuncio**) and some other places in the book, it appears that they were all burned by command; though some were afterward (upon the appearance of better hopes) strangely restored again. Again, in Part II, p. 21, is that horrible imprecation, of which more is said in the Table. Lastly, these remaining papers and records exhibited here were underground, God knows how long; and since then, though carefully preserved, even at the very last, when the worthy owner took care and paid the cost to have them transcribed, they fell into my hands—not unluckily, I hope, for the public good.

<meta>This page contains the errata for the main text and the preface, noting errors caused by the illegibility of the original manuscripts, Edward Kelley's unreliable reporting, and the speed of the printing process.</meta>

# ERRATA: those of the Book,

Many errors will be found in the Book: a good part proceeding (besides ordinary typographical mistakes, even where the best care is used) from the uncorrected state of the Copy. This might have happened, partly through the illegibility of the Original itself in many places, and partly from mistakes in the said Original where it was most legible. The cause of these mistakes and miswriting you may find *Part II, page 159, line 20, etc.* Besides what is said there, it may probably be gathered from *Part II, page 27, line 43, and page 23, line 20,* and other similar places, that *Edward Kelley*, for the most part, when he made reports to *Doctor Dee* of voices and speeches (especially those of some length), did not know what he said himself, and so might the more easily mistake. A good part of the Greek on *Part I, page 27* was misreported and mistaken, as is shown in the Preface (*page...*), and I believe it was never thoroughly understood by *Doctor Dee* himself. It cannot, therefore, be expected otherwise but that there should be many faults in the writing; for which I would not have the innocent (the *Printers* and *Correctors*, I mean) bear more blame than comes to their share. Yet, however, though they are many, most are such (excepting those places where the *Original* was very faulty) as may easily be corrected by an ordinary Reader who is conversant in books of all kinds. Or if not so easily corrected, they are yet such as will not deprive the Reader of the main sense and matter. Some few passages here and there, perhaps, will be found where a reasonable Scholar may be challenged: as *Part II, page 9, line 11, alias vobismet ipsis disperuitis:* which certainly must be read, *alas vobismet-ipsis disprueritis:* there being a manifest (and pertinent) allusion in the words to that allegorical πτεροφυΐα (*wing-breeding: or, bearing:*) of the soul, so famous in the Books of Philosophers, especially Platonists. That very expression is to be found in Plato (or Works commonly ascribed to him): not only πτεροῤῥυεῖν and περὶ ἀποβαλεῖν (which is the same in effect), but even πτεροφυεῖται: *alas confringere*, as it is here. Some such places here and there may be found where the Reader must take some time to consider (especially in what is Latin) if he thinks it worth the while. I have said as much as I think necessary, and as much as my leisure will afford me at this time.

¶ Since this was written, observing that *pages 403 and 404*, where the Latin is very full of faults (far more there than anywhere else that I have observed), I thought it would not be amiss to correct those two pages. The Reader may the better know what he has to do upon such occasions, though I dare say he will not meet with the like again in the whole Book.

The page contains a complex grid known as the "Great Table" or "Tabula Recensa" used in Enochian magic, a system of ceremonial magic based on the 16th-century writings of John Dee and Edward Kelley.

The table consists of a large square filled with individual letters and numbers arranged in a precise grid. It is divided into four main quadrants (the Watchtowers) by a central "Black Cross," visible as the more densely packed horizontal and vertical columns that meet in the center.

1. **Upper Left (Watchtower of the East):** Contains mystical names starting with "sedna..."
2. **Upper Right (Watchtower of the South):** Contains names like "hahrhodno..."
3. **Lower Left (Watchtower of the North):** Contains names starting with "hangli..."
4. **Lower Right (Watchtower of the West):** Contains names like "noxtadg..."

The central cross features specific letter-boxes such as "B I B A G A" and "A G A E A I," which are essential to the Enochian system's hierarchy of angels and spirits. The outer columns of numbers rotate the sequence 1 through 8, a common feature in Dee's cryptographic and magical tables intended for the permutation of names.
</image-desc>

# The HOLY TABLE.

<image-desc>
A large, square ritual diagram known as the "Holy Table" or "Tabula Sancta" from the Enochian system of magic. 

**Border:**
The entire diagram is framed by a border divided into 48 individual squares. Each square contains a unique character from the Enochian alphabet.

**Central Grid:**
At the center of the diagram is a rectangular grid composed of 12 squares, arranged in 3 columns and 4 rows. Each square contains a large, bold Enochian character, with some characters oriented vertically and others horizontally.

**Peripheral Diagrams and Tables:**
Seven smaller sub-diagrams and tables are positioned in the space between the central grid and the outer border:
- **Top center:** A small rectangular table (7 columns wide) filled with combinations of the letters 'B' and 'L' and various numbers.
- **Top left:** A diamond-shaped arrangement of characters featuring the number **7** at the top; the sequences **9 B g** and **8 6 3** in the middle row; **3 6 9** and **L. B 2** in the row below; and the number **8** at the base.
- **Top right:** A circular sigil containing an inscribed inverted triangle. The circle and triangle are populated with numbers (including 3, 4, 7, and 2) and small symbols.
- **Middle left:** A circular diagram containing a cross-hatched grid. The letter **I** appears at the top, bottom, left, and right exterior points of the grid.
- **Middle right:** A small rectangular table containing alphanumeric characters, including letters like **G**, **B**, **L**, and **P**.
- **Bottom left:** A square table containing a dense 7x7 grid of letters and numbers.
- **Bottom right:** A square table containing a 7x7 grid of letters and numbers, including "GB", "T", "666", and "66".

The layout is unified by two diagonal lines that extend from the corners of the central grid to the corners of the outer border.
</image-desc>

# A TRUE
# RELATION
## OF
## Dr. DEE'S *Actions with Spirits.*

### Book of Mysteries (and of the Holy) parallel and new.
->Mortlake MAY 28, 1583.<-

<margin>D. is Dr. Dee, E. K. is Edward Kelley. See the Preface.</margin>
<margin>A. L.</margin>
As I and E. K. sat talking about the noble Pole *Albertus Laski*, the great honor he has obtained here among us, his great popularity with all classes of people—both those who see him or hear of him—and again, how much I was indebted to God that his heart should so fervently favor me, and that he strives so much to suppress and confound the malice and envy of my countrymen against me, so that I might win or recover my reputation to do God better service hereafter, etc.

<margin>Green and red.</margin>
Suddenly, there seemed to come out of my oratory a spiritual creature, like a pretty girl of 7 or 9 years of age, her hair rolled up in front and hanging down very long behind, wearing a gown of say... changeable green and red, and with a train. She seemed to play up and down... and as she moved between them, the books seemed to give way sufficiently, separating one heap from the other while she passed between them. And so I considered, and [recalled] the various reports which E. K. made to me of this pretty maiden, and...

Δ. I said... "Whose girl are you?"
She: "Whose man are you?"
Δ. "I am the servant of God both by my bounden duty, and also (I hope) by His adoption."
A voice: "You shall be beaten if you tell."
"Am I not a fine girl? Let me play in your house; my mother told me she would come and live here."

<margin>Δ.</margin>
Δ. She went up and down with the very lively gestures of a young girl, playing by herself, and several times another person spoke to her from the corner of my study by a large perspective glass, but no one was seen except herself.

"Shall I? I will." (Now she seemed to answer someone in the aforementioned corner of the study).
"I pray you, let me stay a little." [speaking to someone in the aforementioned corner].
Δ. "Tell me who you are?"
"I pray you, let me play with you a little, and I will tell you who I am."
<margin>Jesus.</margin>
Δ. "In the name of Jesus then, tell me."
"I rejoice in the name of Jesus, and I am a poor little girl, Madini. I am the second-to-last of my mother’s children; I have little baby-children at home."
<margin>Madini's own offspring.</margin>
Δ. "Where is your home?"
Ma. "I dare not tell you where I live; I shall be beaten."
Δ. "You shall not be beaten for telling the truth to those who love the truth; all creatures must be obedient to the eternal truth."
<margin>Madini's six sisters.</margin>
Ma. "I promise you I will be obedient. My sisters say they must all come and live with you."

# A true Relation of Dr. Dee's Actions with Spirits.

<margin>Dee.</margin>
Δ. I desire that those who love God should dwell with me, and I with them.
Ma. ...... I love you now that you talk of God.
<margin>Esemeli.</margin>
Δ. Your eldest sister—her name is *Esemeli*.
Ma. ...... My sister is not as short as you make her out to be.
Δ. Oh, I beg your pardon; she is to be pronounced *Esemeli*.

**E. K. She smiles; someone calls her, saying, "Come away, Maiden."**

Ma. ...... I will read over my Gentlewomen first.
My Master Dee will teach me if I say anything amiss.
Δ. Read over your Gentlewomen as it pleases you.
Ma. ...... I have Gentlemen and Gentlewomen; look here.

**E. K. She brings a little book out of her pocket.**
**....... She points to a picture in the book.**

Mad. ...... Is this not a handsome man?
Δ. What is his name?
Ma. ...... By my faith, his name is *Edward*. Look, he has a crown upon his head; my mother says that this man was the Duke of York.

**E. K. She looks at a picture in the book with a coronet in his hand and a crown upon his head.**

Ma. ..... *This was a jolly man when he was King of England.*
Δ. How long has it been since he was King of England?
Ma. ...... Do you ask me such a question? I am but a little maiden. Look, here is his father *Richard Plantagenet*, and his father also.
Δ. What do you call him?
Ma. ...... *Richard*. Surely this was Richard, Earl of Cambridge.

**E. K. She turns the book’s leaves and says:**

Mad. ...... Here is a grim Lord; he makes me afraid.
Δ. Why does he make you afraid?
Ma. ...... He is a stern fellow; I do not know who he is. But this was the Duke of Clarence. This was the father of Richard, Earl of Cambridge. Look, here is Anne, his wife.

**E. K. Turning over the leaf,**

The same was heir to all the Mortimers' lands.
*Edmund* was her brother.
Look, sir, here are the wicked Mortimers.

**E K. She turned over various leaves, and then she said:**

Ma. ...... This same one is Roger Mortimer.
...... My mother says this man was Earl of the Marches.
This same one is his wife.
He gained a great deal of land through her, for she was an heir.
This same one is wild Genvill, her father.

<margin>Pronounced Jenvill.</margin>
Here is a town they call Weobley. Here is Bewdley. Here is Mortimer's Cleobury. Here is wild Wenlock. Here is Ludlow. Here is Stanton Lacy. Genvill's wife was heir to all of these. Here is Hugh Lacy, her father. He wears his hair long, for he was Deputy of Ireland; that makes him look with such a contorted face.
My sister has torn out the other two leaves; I will bring them when you have finished supper.
I pray, do not tell anybody about me.
Δ. We were earnestly called to supper by my people.

->After Supper.<-

<margin>Note.</margin>
Ma, ...... Here is William Lacy, father to Hugh.
Here is Richard, his father. And here is Sir Richard, his father; and here is William, Sir Richard's brother. Here is his journey into France.
Δ. In what year of Christ?

<margin>Her eldest sister. Her sister is to tell the rest.</margin>
Mad. ...... I guarantee you my eldest sister will tell you all. Here is his journey into Denmark.
My sister will come shortly and tell you how he married in Poland, and what offspring this William had.
Δ. I pray you, explain the pedigree down to this *Albert Laski*.
Ma. ...... Alas, I cannot tell what is done in other countries.
Δ. I know you are not restricted to this country, but are universal for all countries in the whole world, which is indeed but one country, or a great city, etc.
Mad. ...... Well, my sister will shortly come and tell you unexpectedly, if you judge these things well that I have spoken. For they are true. For he who sent me is true.

<margin>June 2, 1583.</margin>

**Monday, 4:30 PM**

Δ. We presented ourselves, ready to receive instruction, and did not presume to call my good spiritual minister, but by humble prayer referred everything to God's good pleasure.

**E. K. The golden curtain which covers the whole stone still hangs there, but I hear a voice or sentence repeated three times, like this:**

A voice ...... *Sanctum, Signatum, & ad tempus.* <note>Holy, sealed, and for a time.</note>

Δ. The meaning of this may be understood in various ways, and more than I can imagine; but I would like to know which meaning is for our instruction.

A voice, ...... *Sanctum, quia hoc velle suum; sigillatum quia determinatum ad tempus.* <note>Holy, because this is His will; sealed, because it is determined for a time.</note>

**E. K. Difficult words, but he could not perfectly distinguish them.**

A voice ...... *For a time and for a time (I say) because the consummation of all things is here. All things are at hand, The Seat is prepared. Justice has determined. The Judge is not yet willing. Mercy thrusts itself between the Divinity. But it is said, The Time shall be shortened.*

**E. K. Saw no creature: But the voice came from behind him, over his head, until now: when he saw one standing on the table beside the silk cloth on which the stone stood; he looked like a husbandman dressed entirely in red clothing: red hose tight to his legs, a red jacket, a red buttoned cap on his head, and even red shoes. He asked E. K. how he was doing, and E. K. answered, "Well, I thank God."**

Δ. By your clothing, it seems you have something to say concerning the common people of this realm, and not about advanced academic subjects or sciences. I am desirous to know who sent you? What is your message? And what is your name? For you must have a unique name, as all other creatures do.

Δ. He paused for a good while; whereupon I asked him if he considered my speeches?

...... *I consider your speeches, for I have left nothing behind.*

**E. K. He kneels down and seems to say something; his speech is quick, direct, and ready. He seems to pray in a strange language. I recognized these words among many others: *Oh Gahire Rudna gepbna oh Gahire, etc.***

His countenance was directed toward the stone.

...... *Vestra non mea facio.* <note>I do your things, not mine.</note>

Neither prescribe any form to God's building.
All things shall be brought into a uniform Order.

<margin>Al. a Laski.</margin>

<margin>Notes in Election.</margin>

<margin>A mere untruth in every part of it, and a malicious lie.</margin>
First, a commission was out to attach and apprehend him as a felon for coining money. Secondly, that his wife was gone from Mistress Freeman's house at Blobley, and how Mr. Husey had reported him to be a cozener, and had used very bitter and serious reports of him lately; and that his wife was at home with her mother at Chipping Norton. Whereupon, I, considering his great disorder and the external burdens upon him, and his greater offending of God with his furious impatience internally; and remembering the entire premise of God's service to be performed by us two (if we would be dutiful servants to His Divine Majesty), I was touched with a great pang of compassion—both that any Christian should use such speeches as he used, or be of such a revenging mind and intent as he showed himself to be, and also in respect of my own credit being brought into doubt for embracing the company of such a person, a disorderly person. And thirdly, that the good service of God might thereby be taken from our two executions, to our great danger both in body and soul. Therefore, to do my duty as a man resolute (upon our uniting for God's service) to do for him as for myself, I made <margin>Among friends, all things are common.</margin> God my refuge for comfort, counsel, and help in this great affliction and cross of temptation.

Whereupon, after my vehement and humble prayers for the aforesaid purpose, this voice was heard by E. K.
