$\triangle$ *Note.* Meanwhile, from the angelic speech itself, I recited the prescribed words translated into Latin <note>Dee likely means he read the Latin text aloud or translated the preceding vision for Pucci's benefit</note>, reading quickly to Master Francis Pucci himself; besides, I spoke a few things in passing about the slanders uttered against such actions of ours, etc.

### E. K. Here Uriel appears to me again, and sits in a crystalline Chair with that Book in his lap: in his right hand, however, he holds that Geometric rod: and in his left, that glass Philosophy <note>Likely the scrying stone or a crystal sphere</note>, as before.

URIEL. ..... Since power has been granted to me, and since truth is joined to my ministry (from which I have been made full of light and truth), I will open your eyes, and I will speak the truth itself to you; so that you may shake off that inert mass of your darkness and deep ignorance, and walk in the light with your fathers. Therefore, give ear diligently to my voice, and drink in my words within the liquid of your hearts. So that the juice of your understanding may receive vigor: and you yourselves may flourish with acceptable truth, like chosen servants and Ministers of the MOST HIGH.
The whole world is placed in wickedness; it has become an open workshop of Satan for deceiving the merchants of the earth with every kind of abominable impiety. But what, have you become babbling dealers of such goods? Or carriers of lies and false doctrine into public? Do you estimate it to be a business of light importance to bind the sense, judgment, and mysteries of the Divine Scriptures to the rashness of your imaginations? Do you decide that it is a thing of nothing to sit in judgment against the spirit of God, granting him no place except according to your own prescription?
Is it permitted to you, in the presence of the Son of God, to consume whole days—even unjust years—with the sons of Satan, the lying offspring and deceivers of the world? Have you brought yourselves so thoroughly into the workshop of abomination that you wish to prescribe to the son of God the time of his future coming, and the descent of his Prophets: and the limit of time in which he himself will visit the earth?

> Moses dared to speak nothing except from the mouth of God.
> The Prophets did not explain the Law, but the voice of God did.
> The Son of God did not speak his own words, insofar as he was Flesh, but the words of his father.
> His Disciples taught nothing except from the Holy Spirit.

Do you dare (therefore) to take upon yourselves the duty of teaching, and to open the hidden secrets of the Most High, having been by no means admitted or called to it?
Tell me, have you deserted your trade and the calculations of your money (acquired by fraud), so that you might be Teachers of the word of God?
Are you not ashamed to teach before you yourselves understand?
Indeed, are you not ashamed to lead others astray, before you know how to lead them home?
You are hypocrites, and empty of the Holy Spirit.

You have become liars, and enemies of Christ himself and of his Holy Spirit.
Perhaps you say, "From the reading of the Scriptures, we gain an understanding of them."
But answer me: by the help of which spirit do you gain this understanding for yourselves?
Which Angel appeared to you? Or from which Heaven did you receive your instruction?
It is possible that you will say, "From the Holy Spirit."
O you fool of little understanding! Do you not understand that the Holy Spirit is the Teacher of the Church—of the whole flock and congregation of Christ?
Therefore, if he is the Teacher of the multitude, it follows that any Doctrine which the Holy Spirit teaches—any instruction, document, or understanding—is for the multitude.
Yet, what multitude of people shares your understanding?
Or of which Congregation are you?
Otherwise, you are of the dispersion. Do you say that you are one of some dispersed group? You tell a lie; you are a fugitive.
Truly, look, I teach you: and your error stands before your face.
Whoever would arrive at an understanding of the Scriptures must strive to reach that understanding according to spiritual Ordinance and Tradition.
But from which spiritual tradition have you obtained understanding?
Or according to which Ordinance was the meaning of the Scriptures opened to you?
You will say (perhaps) that you were informed by the holy Fathers, and that you obtained your understanding through the same spirit by which they taught.
You may indeed say so, but it is certain you do not do so.
For which of the ancient Fathers coupled reason with the word of God, or bound the understanding of Scripture to the discipline of the Heathens?
I say to you, that the ancient Fathers were dear to Christ, and participants in heavenly visions and heavenly consolations: which heavenly visions and consolations did not teach them a new interpretation of the Scriptures, but confirmed and illustrated with light the mysteries of the Holy Spirit declared through the Apostles, who laid the foundations of the Church itself; therefore, whatever you can learn from the ancient Fathers, you learn from the Apostles; and whatever you understand from the Apostles, you have indeed from the Holy Spirit. But if you interpret those Fathers according to your own sense and manner, and not according to the sense of the Apostles, you certainly do not have the Holy Spirit, but the spirit of lies.
Therefore, show yourself humble, and fall down before the Lord; set aside reason and cling to the Lord, and labor to understand his word by his Holy Spirit: which Holy Spirit you must of necessity find, and will find, in the visible <note>The Latin text "invisibili" is likely a printing error for "in visibili" (in the visible), given the context of the Apostolic Church.</note> Church until the end of the world.
I will tell you clearly (so that the truth may appear powerfully in the light): whoever is contrary to the will of God—which was handed down to his Church, published indeed by the Apostles, nourished by the Holy Spirit, and imparted to the world, and handed down through Peter to *Rome*, and expressed there by him, and retained and sustained by his successors—this same person is contrary to God and his truth.
*Luther* has received his reward.
*Calvin* has received his.
All the rest, as many as have erred and willfully run into devious ways, separating themselves from the Church and Congregation of Christ obstinately and by the instinct of the Devil (their father), have received their reward.
Against whom the Son of God will pronounce judgment, saying:

> Depart, you Deceivers, into the fire of hell, prepared from the beginning for your Father and his sons.

You rise up among yourselves asserting that the Pope is the Antichrist (for you mark him with this name); he could certainly be an evil man and fall from his vocation, but nevertheless he can never be the Antichrist.
For that Antichrist is he who is the son of the Devil, a man indeed born of flesh and blood from an impious and fraudulent harlot, who will seduce the peoples; and, swollen with his father's power, he will resist God on Earth among men, just as his father had done in Heaven among the Angels, utterly denying God's Omnipotence and opposing himself to him.
<margin>
* Matthew, chapter 16. C. D
</margin>
O you fools and of little understanding, when the keys of Heaven were entrusted to the Apostles: (as if to say) the same authority and power of Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, was given to man to forgive sins and to exclude sinners from Heaven, and when it was also said * to the same Apostles, "Get behind me, Satan," you are not of such intelligence that you are able to look into these mysteries of the Most High.
If the Son of God both commended and also rebuked his disciples, why then cannot a Bishop be judged as both good and evil? If it follows from this that good and evil can exist in a Bishop, by the same reasoning it can be inferred that the nature of Episcopal authority does not depend on that good or evil man, but that this good or evil pertains to the life of the Bishop himself; if he is good, he will reap the benefit of his goodness; but if he is evil, he is a liar, for his own doctrine is contrary to him. Furthermore, if, because of the sins <margin>* Acts 23. A</margin> of men, God has permitted many to sit in the holy place in the spirit of * Ananias, that is indeed because of your sins and rebellious nature, so that you may receive punishment; and his Church would not thereby become obscure or dark.
Therefore, open your eyes and understand, and cling to the Church, for the love of the Church itself, and not for the sake of men. Neither despise the Church because of the iniquities of men.

But submit your necks to the holy yoke and ordinance, which will lead you to that Congregation which is governed by the Spirit of God, in which you will understand the secrets of the Book of God, explained according to the sense of your ancient Fathers: whose understanding was worthy of the Holy Spirit.

You cannot receive authority from yourselves, and without authority you can do nothing.

Therefore, since your authority is nothing, why do you take the works or acts of the Church into your own hands?

<margin>A possessor in bad faith.</margin>
It is one thing to seek an understanding of the Scriptures; and it is another to teach the Scriptures according to one’s own understanding. For he who teaches, teaches by authority: but if he does not have authority, he is a usurper or an intruder.

My brothers, consider yourselves well, and consider that you are children, and that you are not your own masters but belong to another. Therefore, do nothing as if by your own power: but follow (like good children) the footsteps of your Mother, who is a pure Virgin, and is always informed by the wisdom of the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit</note>, who ought to offer food to you (her children), and who ought to educate and instruct you in that way.

Examine yourselves more deeply, whether you are dogs or not.

If you find yourselves not to be in this state, you are not children; if you are not children, you are not sons; if you are not sons, you have no mother; but if you have no mother, you are devourers of that bread which is owed to the children—dog-like, senseless, and you are against God.

### A miracle, and a deed to be remembered forever.

AS E. K. stood at the end of the gallery by his chamber, looking over into the vineyard, he seemed to see the little man, the *Gardener*, in all his usual behavior and clothing, who is the chief workman or overseer of Mr. *Carpio’s* workmen in that same vineyard. He seemed to prune some of the trees very skillfully; at length, he approached under the wall by E. K., and holding his face turned away, he said to him, *I pray you tell the Lord Doctor to come to me.* And so he went away, as if cutting the trees here and there very skillfully, and finally, over the cherry trees by the house on the rock in the garden, he seemed to ascend in a great pillar of fire.

E. K. told his wife to go, as she was in the garden. She came up and brought him word that there was nobody there.

E. K. then came to me and said, "I think there is some wicked spirit that would mock me," and he told me what happened, as was noted before. Then I said, "I will go into the garden," and I told E. K. to come with me. We went down the path that this creature had taken, but we saw nothing. We went to the banqueting house in the vineyard, but that place did not please us; so, we went along the path by the cliff side and sat down on the bank by the great pile of vine-stakes lying at the very south end of the vineyard. And we had not sat there for more than seven or eight minutes before I noticed, under the almond tree and on its south side—being the westernmost almond tree, which stands on the western side of the straight path leading from the north toward the south in the vineyard—I noticed (I say) something like a sheet of fair white paper lying tossed to and fro in the wind. "I rose and went to it, and (to the praise of God’s truth and power) there I found three of my books "lying, which had been so thoroughly burned on the tenth day of April last.

1 The three books were, *The Book of Enoch.*
2 The 48 *Angelic Keys.*
3 And the third was the *Book of my collection of the thirty Aires, and entitled <term>Liber Scientiæ terrestris auxilii & victoriæ</term>.* <note>The Book of Knowledge of Earthly Help and Victory.</note>

Thereupon, as E. K. came toward me, I fell on my knees giving great thanks to Almighty God, and E. K. did the same; his mind and body were marvelously affected at the sight of the "said books, which showed no sign that they had ever been in the fire—neither in color nor "smell, nor was anything missing.

And after we had sat for half an hour under the aforementioned almond trees, praying to God and wondering at the miracle, suddenly the very same gardener-like person appeared by us, but with his face somewhat turned away, and nothing about him seemed to invite a greeting, as is the custom. He said, *Kelley, follow me.* E. K. went, and I sat still, awaiting his return.

This gardener went before E. K., and his feet seemed not to touch the ground by a foot's height. And as he went before E. K., the doors seemed to open before him; he led him up the great stairs on the left hand by the vineyard door, and so in at his own chamber door where E. K. has his new study. Then the door leading out of that room to the stairs opened by itself, and he went up those stairs, and at length brought him to the furnace mouth where all the books and papers had been burned on the 10th day of this April. And coming there, the spiritual creature seemed to set one of his feet on the post on the right hand outside the furnace mouth, and with the other to step to the furnace mouth, and so to reach into the furnace (the bricks being now pulled away which stopped the mouth of the furnace, all except for one brick's thickness). As he reached into the furnace, there appeared a great light, as if there had been a window in the back of the furnace; and also to E. K., the hole—which was no larger than the thickness of a single brick—now seemed more than three or four bricks wide. And so, over his shoulder backward, he reached out and handed to E. K. all the rest of the remaining books, except for the book from which the last action was cut and Francesco Pucci's recantation. Also, all the rest of the papers which were not delivered out at that time appeared to E. K. in the furnace.

That being done, he told E. K. to go, and said he should have the rest afterward. He went before in a little fiery cloud, and E. K. followed with the books under his arm all along the gallery, and came down the stairs by Francesco Pucci's chamber door. Then his guide left E. K., and he brought the books to me at my place under the almond tree.

*See also, that you do not disclose my hand among you, lest I then rise up against you.*

*For, behold, you are yet in the Wilderness. I, therefore, am silent.*

*To William, however (hereafter), all things may be known and made manifest. If any other man seeks you, you do not know him.*

*For you live within the silence of the Highest.*

*The rest that is missing shall be restored to you: even to the least and last letter.*

*Live, therefore, together as in the hands of your Protector.*

*And do not doubt that I will be merciful to him who is sick through his infirmity: yes, and to his generation as I have promised. And the sin which remains in his father's house, and in his house for many generations, I will mercifully blot out.*

*Do not doubt; my peace (who am peace, the beginning and the ending) shall always be among you.*

---

$\triangle$ We read all and had a long discourse about it all, and at last, I asked thus.

**Voice** ..... *That which is said of him, say that, $\triangle$, to him.*
*Move no more questions.*

<column-break/>

$\triangle$ What shall I say to *Rosenberg* of your present merciful dealing and intent toward him?

<column-break/>

> $\triangle$ Benedicite Domino omnia opera ejus, laudate illum omnes Creaturæ ejus: laudent illum Angeli ejus, laudent illum Sancti ejus: ille solus est Omnipotens, ille solus est Sanctus, ille Protector nostri, Illuminator & Consolator noster est. Cinguli omnis honor & gloria. **Amen.**

## M E M O R A N D U M.

1586. May 1.

On May day after dinner I went over the water (being brought to the water side in Lord *Rosenberg's* coach, with *Jacobus Merschick* with me) to Lord *Rosenberg's* gardens and lodging by the water-side, where he came to meet me by appointment. To whom, when I had read in Latin (*extempore*) the things that concerned him, I asked him what he had done since the time of my being with him, so that I might better understand these words spoken to him and of him.

He said that he had often prayed since then to God for the forgiveness of his sins, and to open his eyes to how he might serve him; and to make it evident to him whether he is to marry or not, and where, or into what stock or kindred. And if it were his divine will, that he might receive comfort and instruction through me, and regarding these and such matters; and he had also prayed somewhat earnestly for his master the Emperor, that he might bend himself to enjoy God's favor; yes, for his own marriage and the amending of his loose life. While he yet sat at dinner today at the Archbishop's table, his heart and thoughts were very much upon it, etc.

At these words of his, I rejoiced much to perceive the work of the Highest in the hearing of his prayer faithfully prayed, and that the answer which I read to him was so fitly applied to his prayer, as he himself also perceived with great comfort and spiritual joy. He entreated much that I would pray to God that the Emperor might be restored to the favor of God, as he was when I declared my message to him from the Highest. I answered that whatever the God of Heaven and Earth should appoint me to say or do to his Majesty, I most willingly rejoice in the faithful doing of it: and that it was my duty (as a Christian) to pray for his Majesty: but I should not make a promise that my prayer would be heard, but would highly rejoice if his Imperial Majesty would so conduct himself in God's judgment as might be meritorious in the sight of our Redeemer.

<margin>
The vow and promise of William Ursinus, Vice-regent of Bohemia.
</margin>

Such words and matters as these passed between us. And he said that he would in all points fulfill the advice and warning of God expressed in this Action, and would marry a maiden as he was commanded. And this day he did acknowledge and account himself a happy man. And concerning our mutual bond by means of each being given to the other by the God of Heaven and Earth, he vowed and promised that he would regard it in all points to the best of his skill and power, etc.

These and other such good seeds for the service of God being sown between us, he went toward his palace in the Court, and I to the water-side, and so over to the coach waiting for me, and so came home. God be praised.

->### MEMORANDUM.<-

The Lord *Rosenberg* sent Mr. *Jacob Menschik* with this Letter to me.

## To the Magnificent Lord John Dee, into his own hands.

## Magnificent Lord, Respected and Dearest Father.

I was glad for those things which you told me. For I have known that the pious Father and merciful Lord has heard my prayer. Therefore, I have greatly desired that I might be able to read, re-read, and always have them before my eyes as often as possible; by the love of God, I pray that you send me a transcript of those words which were read to me and pertain to me. Not only will I be much gratified, but I will also be greatly consoled.

I besides beseech your Lordship that you would be willing to pray for me continually, so that God may confirm what he has worked in us: and direct all our counsels, works, actions, and even our thoughts to the praise and glory of his most holy name, the benefit of many, and the salvation of our soul. Nor should your Lordship—out of your fatherly love with which (as I hope) you regard me—cease to always advise and inform me in all things which both should and can be done by me for the honor of God and your benefit. You will do a thing highly pleasing to me and worthy of and consistent with my expectation. And with these words, I commend myself to your petitions and prayers, as well as to your fatherly love and heart. May your Magnificent Lordship fare very well. Sunday, Cantate [the fourth Sunday after Easter], the year 1586.

*May* 6. Being Tuesday, I began my journey toward the *Valkenaw glass-house*, and the *Leipzig fair*.
There are various *Valkenaws*: one by *Eger*, or *Elbogen*, not far from *Carlsbad*, westward from *Prague* about 18 *Bohemian miles*; another in *Bohemia*, about 11 or 12 miles from *Prague*, northerly, a mile from *Krebitz*, and two miles from *Leipa*, and a mile from *Kamnitz*.

---

->### NOTE.<-

*May* 11. I came to *Leipzig* on Sunday the 11th of *May*, and was lodged at *Peter Hans Swartz’s* house. I found *Laurence Overton* (with much difficulty), an *English* merchant, to whom my wife (last year) had shown no little friendship—both to himself and to *Thomas*, his partner’s servant—at the time of his lying sick in our house, etc., at *Prague*. He came from *England* at Mid-Lent; he confessed that *Edmond*, my servant, had been with him many times at his house, and that he thought he would arrive with the next ships after his departure from *England*, which were then to arrive within 16 days.

I perceived by his various express sayings that he was but a hollow friend to me, and seemed half afraid to deal either with me or my man.

There, I also found a courteous gentleman called Mr. *Francis Evers*, the son of Lord *Evers* of the *North*. And omitting the rehearsal in these records of all other matters (I mean those matters which happened notably to me at *Leipzig* and in this journey, or which I did myself), one letter which I wrote to the Queen of *England’s* Secretary, the Right Honorable Sir *Francis Walsingham*, follows.

## Right Honorable SIR,

Although I have (almost) in vain come a hundred miles (from Prague to this *Leipzig* Fair) hoping to meet my servant there with an answer to my former letters, sent last November to her Majesty (at which time I also wrote to your Honor and various others). And thus I had hoped to send word again from this *Leipzig* most speedily as the occasion served. And now I find neither servant, nor letter from him, nor any word of mouth; yet despite all this, and whatever the hindrance or delay of it may be (whether the withholding of my letters from her Majesty, or the many urgent and most weighty public affairs hindering or delaying her Majesty’s most gracious, discreet, and wise resolution in this matter, or whatever other occasion has caused and does cause this long and remarkable delay in receiving an answer); despite all this, I thought it good, before I put away my coach, to visit and most humbly salute your Honor very faithfully, dutifully, and sincerely, with the same great goodwill that my letter written some years ago to your Honor (which was then a stumbling block to your Honor and others because of the strangeness of its phrasing) expressed. So it is, Right Honorable, that the merciful providence of the Most High, declared in his great and abundant graces upon me and mine, is so wonderful and mighty that very few, unless they are eyewitnesses, can believe it. Therefore, how hard they are to be believed there, where my whole life and actions were interpreted in a contrary sense, and a sentence of death was contrived and decreed against an innocent man, anyone can easily judge.

I am forced to be brief. That which *England* suspected was also here, for these two years, almost (secretly) in doubt, in question, and in Imperial and Royal consultation; it was discussed, pried, and peered into by honorable spies fawning about me and by others. And at length, both the chief Roman power and the Imperial dignity are brought to that point, resolutely, that they are partly sorry for being so late to correct their erroneous judgment against us and of us, and they seek means to deal with us so that we might favor both the one and the other. And partly, they have sent to *Rome* for as great an authority and power as can be devised; and likewise here, all other means and ways are contrived to see how, by force or for fear, they may make us glad to follow their whims. But it is all in vain, for we do not fear human force, as I have plainly and often declared to the Princes. And we will not favor any except in pure truth and godliness (my words may seem very marvelous in your Honor’s ears, but mark the end: we have had—and shall have—no children to deal with). I have very often, and at many of their requests

I thought it good to commit this much, very rhapsodically (yet faithfully), as a word to the wise (*tanquam dictum sapienti*), to the safe and speedy delivery of a young merchant here called Lawrence Overton. And my commission from above is not so large: "He who can understand, let him understand" (*Qui potest capere, capiat*).

Sir, I trust I shall have justice for my house, library, goods, and revenues, etc. Do not disdain, nor fear to show favor to your poor innocent neighbor. If you send Master Thomas Digges to me on her Majesty’s behalf, his faithfulness to her Majesty and my personal liking of the man shall produce some piece of good service. But her Majesty would have been better to have spent or given away in alms *a million in gold* than to have lost some past opportunities. No human reason can limit or determine God’s marvelous means of proceeding with us. He has made a Paul out of Saul (E.K. <note>Edward Kelley</note>); but yet, he is now and then visited with a pang of human frailty. ## To my most Illustrious and Magnificent Lords, most Worthy of Honor.

**T**he blessing of God the Father, and pure grace and mercy through the sole merit of Jesus Christ, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, confirm us with all Christians who, with great zeal for His glory, suffer the cross, tribulation, and persecution from the rancid and rotten Babylonian whore, in the most turbulent ocean of this world; so that by the example of Jesus Christ who is in the Father, and by the power and help of the Holy Spirit, we may be able to endure all these things patiently for the glory of His name and the salvation of our souls. Amen.

It will perhaps seem strange to your Lordships that I, a stranger, write to you who are unknown to me. You will attribute a good part of this fault to the most just grief which I have conceived from a rumor spread and brought to me concerning your Lordships. For I cannot marvel enough at the persistent zeal of that Babylonian beast <note>Referring to the Papacy.</note>, which leaves nothing unattempted, moving every stone, by which it strives not only to harm but to utterly destroy men of your nation, especially those who are pious and lovers of God. For on the eleventh day of this month, the Papal Nuncio offered a petition (as they call it) to his Imperial Majesty, in which he suggests that your Lordships are involved in <term>Necromancy</term> and other prohibited arts, and gravely accuses you with other slanders. I could have obtained copies of this petition, but I was informed of this matter too late, and it is neither safe nor without suspicion to ask the person who translated it from the Italian into the Latin language. Therefore, since I know for certain that all these things are empty regarding your Lordships as Christian men and Philosophers, I have seen fit to write this letter both to support and to warn you, so that they may find your Lordships more prompt and ready to respond. I ask, therefore, that you receive it in the same spirit in which it was written—namely, that of an upright and sincere Christian. Farewell, and commend me to Christ in your prayers.

### P O S C R I P T.

<margin>
Julius Ascanius, seventh from Verdeman.
</margin>

### *To the most Illustrious Prince and Lord, the Lord Wilhelm Ursinus, hereditary Lord of the Noble House of Rosenberg, Lord in Krumlov, Knight of the Golden Fleece, Privy Councilor to his Imperial Majesty, and Supreme Burgrave in the Kingdom of Bohemia, etc. My most Honorable Lord and Patron.*

Illustrious Prince, nothing more pleasing could be reported to me by the Magnificent Lord Schomberg than that your Highness continues to enjoy good health. Meanwhile, I have been tossed about on a varied, diverse, and complicated journey, through mountains, valleys, densest forests, open fields, and through deep snow that was almost impassable for us. Yet (with the Most High always protecting us), we have at last returned safe and sound, with both the horses and your Highness’s carriage unharmed. For this prosperous success, we give the highest thanks to the Most High, and we confess that infinite thanks are owed from us to your Highness. 

While I was absent, that *Apostolic Nuncio* <note>The Papal Nuncio, Germanico Malaspina.</note> has begun to believe some falsehood or other too easily and to complain rashly, or perhaps to devise perverse things of his own accord. Truly, if they continue in this way (having already had a sufficiently accurate experience of us for two years), those who ought to surpass all men in piety and wisdom—at least among the common people—instead declare themselves to be the most envious, malicious, and perverse of all men: thirsty for human blood, proud, executioners of the innocent, and deadly slanderers of those who are pious in Christ, etc. Truly, I say, we will be forced to shake the dust from our shoes and betake ourselves to other parts of the world. And unless we had that consideration for your Highness which we ought, and unless we considered ourselves protected by your Highness's armed guard (as it were)—besides that invincible, invisible army of God the Best and Greatest—we would immediately attempt to depart from this kingdom. 

His Imperial Majesty should also take care that somehow, and very quickly, it might be clear to this whole Kingdom that we two are not only true Catholics, but also most loving of true piety and Christian peace. It is not necessary for me to pour out more in these letters through the fervor of my spirit. But let us both look back most diligently and circumspectly at the inestimable Gift of God, which he has conferred on us both. For we are as if three. But in one God, we ought to be as one man. Note this mystery: *J. D. E. K. W. R.* <note>John Dee, Edward Kelly, Wilhelm von Rosenberg.</note> For he who has me, also has *E. K.*; and him whom I have as mine, he also is to be considered as belonging to my *E. K.* 

May that Almighty God who created all things join your Illustrious Highness to us as a minister and co-operator of His divine Justice and Glory, and preserve you for a very long time.

->Prague, May 26, 1586.<-

*Your Illustrious Highness’s most faithful servant in Christ.*

->John Dee.<-

### To the Most Invincible and Most Powerful, His Sacred Imperial Majesty,
### King of Hungary, Bohemia, etc., etc.

**F**or several weeks now, Most Invincible and Most Gracious Emperor, various rumors have been ringing in our ears that certain serious and destructive accusations are being prepared against me and my associate, to be presented to your Sacred Imperial Majesty—or perhaps they have already been presented. Furthermore, we hear that your Sacred Imperial Majesty has been almost led, by the persuasions of certain people, to conceive some bad and dangerous opinion of us. Therefore, we most humbly beseech your Sacred Imperial Majesty that (by your Imperial authority being interposed) you would graciously deign to command that a copy of whatever libel has been presented against us be accurately transcribed word-for-word and delivered to us. For in this way, by comparing our responses to the specific points of the accusation fabricated against us, your Sacred Imperial Majesty will very quickly and clearly understand what can or should be decided and determined in these matters, according to justice, for the honor of God and the benefit of the Christian Commonwealth.

And of this we are most certain, God willing (which even now, and for far too long, remains hidden from your Sacred Imperial Majesty due to the negligence of some and against our will): that we can be far more useful and acceptable both to your Sacred Imperial Majesty’s person and to the Christian Commonwealth than all our present adversaries, whoever they may be. The truth itself will show this, if it can find such favor before your Imperial Majesty’s own ears as to be graciously heard. May the Greatest and Best God most abundantly illuminate your Sacred Imperial Majesty with His Divine grace and, with His outstretched arm, make you a most triumphant Emperor against the most atrocious enemies of Christ.

Specifically from the Imperial, as well as the Hungarian and Bohemian Royal Majesty, our most gracious Lord, it is announced to Doctor John Dee, Englishman: That His Majesty, for urgent, serious, and reasonable causes, has decided that neither he nor his associates shall be tolerated or permitted to stay any longer within His Majesty's Kingdom of Bohemia, nor in any other of his kingdoms, principalities, or lands. Therefore, it is His Majesty’s final will and earnest command that he, together with his wife, children, and all his followers, as well as his associate and subordinate <note>Referring to Edward Kelley</note>, upon pain of His Majesty’s severe and inevitable punishment and displeasure, shall leave this place within the next six consecutive days. Immediately thereafter, they must depart from the said Kingdom of Bohemia and His Majesty’s other kingdoms, principalities, and lands, and shall not be found or encountered there in the future. This is so that His Majesty is not compelled to apply the severity and punishment—which he would rather avoid—due to any disobedience or transgression by him or his followers. His Majesty did not wish to withhold this from him for his formal notice. This is His Majesty's firm will and intention. Decreed in the Imperial Majesty's Secret Council. Prague, May 29, Anno 1586.

E. Waldstein Seifeld.

<header>A true relation of Dr. Dee his Actions, with spirits, &c.</header>

*In the year 1586, on June 18th, in Erfurt, Thuringia, the most illustrious Lord Rosenberg sent Johann Carpion to us with his letters, especially so that he might understand the will of God regarding his future wife and other matters, etc. But I was already in Kassel in Hesse, and Mr. Edward Kelley was in Erfurt. He, concerning the questions and petitions of the Illustrious Lord, was commanded by God to place a clean sheet of paper upon the Altar before a Priest celebrating Mass. This* <margin>Admonition.</margin> *$\Delta$ <note>Dee’s symbol for himself or his office</note> did on the year and day written above, in the morning in the Monastery of the Minor Order of Saint Francis, between the hours of 6 and 7, while a Senior Monk was celebrating Mass. And when the Mass was finished, those things which follow were found beautifully written on the paper. But on the following day, after they had been transcribed for the Illustrious Prince,* <margin>During the time of our exile.</margin> *all the lines and letters immediately vanished, and nothing remained visible on that paper afterward, etc.*

---

All the nations of the earth, called to Judgment, shall stand before the Tribunal. For a rebellious people, too much devoted to the pleasure of this world, has long been consumed by the wrath of my fury: so much so that there must be no turning aside, neither to the left nor to the right, but to the fulfillment of my will. Blessed is he who is obedient to me and the commands of my father and is adorned with perseverance.

But cursed is he who is lying in his works and destroys my word: because he will be a scandal to many and a shame to the peace of my Gospel.

I have appointed you, *William* <note>Wilhelm von Rosenberg</note> (because you have joined your hands to me), as *David* to slay *Goliath*, and in appointing you, I have brought you in.

Use the world, therefore, for my glory, and raise up your body in me, to place my justice in its proper seat, and to utterly trample down and root out the most wicked and foul pride of those who have turned my seat into a footstool of blasphemy and abomination.

For you shall be blessed in the strength of my hand and spirit, because your prayers have been heard. Do not, therefore, neglect the time of your visitation: but rage with zeal and the sharpest indignation, and take as a wife the virgin joined to your walls <note>Likely referring to a neighbor or someone close to his estate</note>, prepared for your loins and your old age; love her dearly, and in loving her, cherish her, so that my promised blessing in you and in her may be made manifest.

Beware, furthermore, lest you allow those my servants whom I have prepared to help you to be snatched from your hands—or like sheep from your fold—by the evil arts and iniquity of others, whether through your negligence or your fear. For who shall steal away that which was given by me?

Think, therefore, and watch with care over what has been injured until now.

For I will break the bridle of Satan and your enemies.

The blessing of the Father and my Spirit, and consolation from me (to whom all power is subject), be with you and upon you.

Finally, warned against sins, cease from them, so that when you speak my word, your life may be supported by my light and grace.

---

## M E M O R A N D U M.

<margin>Mr. Francis Pucci. May 6, 1586.</margin>
*Let it be remembered that Mr. Francis Pucci, a Florentine, whom I left in our house at Prague when I went to Leipzig, had in the meantime been at Frankfurt am Main. He left Prague about the same day that the Bishop of Piacenza, the Apostolic Nuncio, presented a libel to the Emperor against us containing most horrible untruths, etc. At his departure from Prague, he had that Nuncio's blessing, etc. In the meantime, and after his return to Prague again, it happened that on the 30th of last May, I received the Emperor's command for me, my companion, and all my household to depart within six days from Prague, and consequently from all his kingdoms, duchies, and lands. This we did, and we came to Erfurt in Thuringia, and sometimes to Kassel, to which we had moved our goods and family because the Senators of Erfurt would not grant us permission to rent any house there. This was attempted by the Lord Schonberg in the name of the Lord Rosenberg, but a refusal was received, and it was also tried again by me and Edward Kelley on July 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14. And on Tuesday (the 15th of June), Doctor Curtz brought word from the Senate that they would not grant our request; yet, nonetheless, if the Lord Rosenberg would send to them again regarding the matter, they would think better of it, etc.*

*Now remember that Francis Pucci came to Erfurt on Thursday after our supper, July 10 (New Style), on horseback, on a horse which he had bought at the Naumburg fair, etc.*

*On July 11th, he conversed with Edward Kelley and me, saying that he thought we might obtain favor to return to Prague again if we wished.*

*He said that he had found this Apostolic Nuncio more courteous than Malaspina, of whom he also reported that it was credibly informed that he was deeply offended that we gave him no more honorable title in our speeches to him than "Your Most Reverend Paternity."*

*This Pucci framed his talk to persuade us to think well of this Bishop of Piacenza—that he was charitable toward us and sorry that we were so uncourteously treated, and that he meant nothing else in his suit to the Emperor against us but that we might be examined, and you being found*

->N O T E.<-

The Lord *Rosenberg* told us that when he (on our behalf) advised the Emperor of his error committed in our banishment, the Emperor answered that this *Nuncio*, from his first audience, urged so vehemently against us, and also that the Pope had sent a commandment by letter to him to deliver us and send us to *Rome*, so that he was forced, in a way, to do as he did. But if the commandment or his decree were to be made again, it should not pass; or if this *Nuncius Apostolicus* had not sent this decree away to *Rome*, he should not have sent it, etc. I note this in respect of the contradiction between the *Nuncio's* assertion and the Emperor's regarding our harsh treatment.

On the aforementioned eleventh day of *July*, the aforementioned *Fr. Pucci*, to prove his intended persuasion of the *Nuncio's* good meaning toward us, and to make us believe that great benefit would result from our going to *Rome*, brought to us a writing in his own hand which he read to us; at the hearing of it, we marveled much for many reasons. I asked him then why the *Nuncio* had not signed this writing. "It is all the same," he said, "as to that." "Has he heard this read?" I asked. "Yes," he said, "he has heard me read this three several times as I read it unto him." "And if you like it," he said, "where his power does not serve him to perform as much as is specified in the writing, he will find and use means to obtain it from his Holiness." "Well," I said, "take a copy of this, *Mr. Kelly*," for I was riding toward *Salfeild* to acquire a house. Thereupon he said, "Contented." "I think it more proper to save and keep the original itself," said *E. K.* "Well," said *Pucci*, and so the original was delivered to *E. K.*

->N O T E.<-

After 10 o'clock that same Friday, being the eleventh day of this month, after breakfast I rode toward *Salfeild* concerning the house of the Earl *Albert* of *Swartzenberg*, etc.

But after I was out of *Erffurd* until my return, I was so sorely vexed in mind to think of *Pucci's* return to our company—as much for his unquiet nature in disputations as for his blabbing of our secrets without our permission or approval, or any good coming of it, either in God's service or to our credit, but rather the contrary resulting (though not by his intent, but either by his indiscreet handling of it or by those who improperly heard him), etc. And also for his household behavior, which was not acceptable to our wives and family; and also because we were warned that he should be cut off from our company, etc. And chiefly, now to consider that he had laid <margin>A bait.</margin> such a bait for us with our mortal enemy to entrap us with fair, fawning words—which by no means the Emperor would consent to do before by his authority, but rather to put us out of his kingdoms, etc. And imagining that he was <margin>A spy.</margin> a powerful spy upon us for this *Nuncius Apostolicus* and his adherents, so that now he might perceive what we had done until now, what we were doing, and what we intended to do; and considering that he urged from our hands an answer to the previous writing, wherein also lay a trap—for either in not answering it, or refusing to grant some points of it, or in our consenting to the whole, this *Nuncio* would use the matter against us to our great disadvantage. Thus being tormented in mind during my absence, as to how we might be rid of this *Fr. Pucci* by quiet and honest means, I devised a plan to write to this *Nuncio* to know if this writing were of his contriving only, or of *Pucci’s* contriving only, or jointly, or if at least the writing were according to his will and offer to us, and so to send him away; wherein he could make no refusal. I intended not to make him privy to the content of my letter; and in the time of his absence, I hoped that some good way and better means would appear or occur upon which we might rely, etc. Thus I note my thoughts and reflections during the time of my absence.

I returned to *Erphurd July* 13 at 5 o'clock in the afternoon.

I found *Fr. Pucci* eager to have an answer to the aforementioned writing, and very much urging this *Roman* voyage, using arguments from our actions, such as that God said we should go to *Rome* within a certain months’ time; that we ought to obey the *Roman* Bishop and to love him, etc. I replied and said that he was not to urge God upon any of His sayings to us, but to refer all to His most free disposition; His will was to be done and not ours; God was not bound to us, etc. He answered very vehemently and often, "God is most bound to us, and God said we were to go to Rome, and I have believed and will believe, and I will not believe otherwise unless God tells me, not us," etc. "Well," we said, "God has delivered to us His meaning in that expression, which we also inform you of: that it is not meant (by the speech) that we shall physically go to *Rome*"; and so I broke off that reasoning of his. And I told him that we marveled that he should urge this *Roman Voyage* so violently and eagerly, more than we did; it pertained to us as much as to him, etc. The same day I told him that he had previously offended God with his curiosity in our affairs in ways that did not pertain to his calling, and he may well remember his repentance therein and the forgiveness he obtained. Now he had offended much more in his prying curiosity, and almost in a conspiracy against us with our mortal enemy, this Apostolic Nuncio, whom he fawns upon and in whose favor he remains. This Nuncio joins and counsels with him in our affairs, and dares to prescribe to us what we must do in such weighty matters as our journey to Rome. He has framed a document accusing us indiscriminately of heresy and wicked magic—falsely in the first part, and in a way that is dangerous to our lives and shameful, at the very least, in the other. Furthermore, he requires, urges, and in a manner argues in God’s name for obedience regarding our past actions. Therefore, he has separated himself from us and has set himself against us, etc.

With great vehemence, he said he intended nothing but well toward us and acted as a scout with this Nuncio on our behalf. "We require none," I said, "nor do we need any, for God sees all and does all for our benefit, if we will constantly love and serve him." To be brief, he would seem to want to be thought well of for his zealous goodwill and fidelity toward us in all his doings and sayings. The truth of this God knows, to whom we commit the cause between him and us.

### The Copy of the writing before specified.

SID. Johannes Dee, D. Eduardus Kelleus, & Fr. Puccius, volent ire Romam, ut conferant cum Summo Pontifice de suis Revelationibus, venerantes eum tanquam Sancti Petri Successorem & Christi in terris Vicarium Illust. & Reverend. Episcopus Placentinus Apostolicus Nuncius apud Cæsaream Majestatem, dabit illis Literas commendationis, ut per totum iter, & Romæ, humanissime summaque charitate tractentur, & in suis necessitatibus juventur: Ac præterea authoritate Apostolica absolvet eos & liberabit ab omni culpa & pœna, quam meriti essent in vita ante acta, ob artes Magicas exercitatas, hæreses, falsasque opiniones ab eis sparsas, aut fictas, verbis aut scriptis, aut aliis rationibus; ob libros prohibitos lectos aut scriptos, sive ob aliud quodvis crimen, cujus accusari aut argui possent in foro sancto Inquisitionis, aut in foro quod Contentiosum vocant; aut in quovis alio foro Pontificiæ ditionis: Ne quis ob ullum peccatum aut scelus quantumvis atrox, quod illi admiserint ante hoc iter susceptum, eis unquam facessere negotium, aut molestus esse possit, aut ullo modo inquirere, aut ipsos accusare præsumat.

For a better basis for making any kind of answer to this, I asked the same Father Pucci after supper on Tuesday, July 15 (since I had drafted a letter to answer the substance of the letter or writing recorded here), whether this letter was written and sent to us with the consent of this Apostolic Nuncio, so as to know our answer, or not. He seemed unwilling now to directly affirm the Nuncio's consent. We replied that he had already told us that he had read it three times to the said Nuncio, and that the Nuncio liked it well, and that it was a marvel that he would now find it strange to affirm the same thing again—seeing that I had now (according to his purpose) written a plain, perfect, and humble answer to the same letter, and much more matter that was true and necessary for this Nuncio to know. "Well," he said, "It is with his consent to this extent: if you are willing to go to Rome, he will strive to provide those things contained in the same letters," etc. "Well," I said (you must understand that my talk with him was always in Latin, though recorded here in English), "if he means well toward us, and in unfeigned charity, he will not be offended by my answer, the copy of which follows."

Informed by divine guidance some years ago, and then called out of *England*, we have not only escaped many and great dangers of the sea by the most strong hand of Almighty God and miraculously, but also, being freed until now from the various fraudulent and cruel plots and attempts of men against us and our lives, we sing praises and thanks to our same God with a grateful mind, a joyful mind, and truly a mind most loving of the Christian, Catholic, and Apostolic Religion, and (by God's confirming grace) a mind that will remain most steadfast. But behold, nevertheless, those who are considered legitimate sons of our same pious mother (the Holy Catholic Church) were suddenly procuring, by *Imperial* mandate, a certain exile or banishment for us—their brothers, who were living among them and before them in *Prague* in all modesty, quiet, peace, and civil justice. No cause for such a violent mandate was declared to us at all, neither privately nor publicly; but by common and courtly report made to us, we understood from a certain petition exhibited to his sacred *Imperial* Majesty by you, that the greatest indignation and, as it were, a blazing anger of the *Emperor* had been stirred up against us. Whence from the *Bohemian* Chancery, a most bitter *mandate was sent to us (in the name of his sacred *Imperial* Majesty)—with no cause or legitimate reason for the same mandate expressed in it—that within the next six following days, I, my companion, our wives, all my children, and even our infant *Michael* (born and baptized in *Prague* and still hanging at his mother's breasts), also my menservants and maidservants, and finally all my people and household, should depart from *Prague* itself, and consequently from the entire kingdom of *Bohemia* and any other kingdoms, Duchies, and lands of his sacred *Imperial* Majesty, never to return to them, under the danger of a terrible punishment to be inflicted. 

We, however, without any delay, prepared ourselves to obey this *Imperial* mandate faithfully and humbly. We saw to it that our movable goods, the equipment for our pilgrimage, both books and household items, were cast into two large wagons. Of our remaining goods, we gave one part to friends and dispersed and distributed another part to the poor. But another part, for reasons not unpleasing to God, you should know was destroyed by us the day before this departure of ours. Yet the best part, by Divine command, on the tenth day of *April* (when we were also divinely forewarned about all this affliction and persecution of ours, and others yet to come), *we committed to the bright flames of a fire; when those things of that same best part, which no natural or common fire could ever hurt or consume, were received by visible angelic ministry out of the smoking flames themselves into Divine or Angelic invisible custody.* But the greatest treasury of Divine books, then and there (by the diligent labor of two witnesses still living), was entirely converted into ashes and embers by the flames; it will receive a renovation, restoration, and a kind of regeneration or resurrection by the Divine hand in due time. 

Finally, we leave the Chapel untouched, with the altar which we desired to be consecrated to the almighty Trinity (being half-finished). I, indeed, with my companion, our wives, my children, and the rest of our exiled or banished ones, being carried away in three *carriages*, began this migration enjoined upon us on the appointed day. And not yet having departed from the borders of the *Roman* Empire, we so order our steps, and for the rest (God favoring and governing) will so order them, that it may appear clearly to the whole Christian world that we are able, or at least willing, to endure these things (whatever they may be) patiently: and that we are most ready to render to God the things that are God's, and to the *Emperor* the things that are the *Emperor's*. Also, that we are the most obedient and humble sons of the holy Catholic Church, and that we are and will be as observant of the Roman Pontiff and other Catholic ecclesiastical prelates, in Christ and for Christ's sake, as he who is to be the Judge of the living and the dead has not infrequently warned us in various ways. But to your Illustrious and most Reverend Lordship, we wish this good from God: that through your secondary meditations (concerning our whole cause), a just account may be taken of our innocence, sincerity, and faithful conversation (before God and men) in that *Bohemian* Republic; and that such a full restitution be made to my honest reputation and standing (without which I do not even desire to live) that such

...let it hereafter be undoubtedly declared to be such as (before your petition against us was presented to his Imperial Majesty) for 30 years (and more) in almost all the Universities, Kingdoms, and Provinces of the Christian world (by God's immense goodness, most abundant grace, and singular providence) it can be confirmed by no obscure testimonies to have existed. From these few sparks of the truth of the history itself, the wisdom of Your Most Illustrious and Reverend Lordship could draw or kindle a great light for itself: to judge us, the affections of our minds, the progress and state of our so wonderful and still incredible affairs, and finally to weave no trivial conjectures for itself concerning the future outcome of all these things. For we depend in all our affairs upon the only Almighty God, both true and living, and are directed and protected by him. After this letter was written and read to *E. K.*, he liked it for the quiet and modest tone it maintained—unlike what he said to *Fr. Pucci* he would have used, or had used in a letter he had also written. However, he decided not to send his own letter, thinking my aforementioned letter might be sufficient for our situation. He talked with *Fr. Pucci* about this letter, and *Fr. Pucci* said he would gladly see and read it. *E. K.* told him that I intended not to let him read it. Then *Pucci* said he would not deliver it. 

During a conversation with *Fr. Pucci* about this letter, I told him that I had written a letter with a sufficient general answer to the *Nuncio's* request and the offer he had brought us in writing, and I summarized the main contents of the letter for him. Then he said, "Since you write about the books being burned, why do you not write to him about their recovery, as I now understand from both of you that they are restored? It will be a disgrace to you if the *Nuncio* learns more from others than from yourself." 

I am not concerned about that. *What I have written, I have written*, and I know the truth of my writing. And they are not all restored, as far as I know. Whatever he receives from my hands, he can be assured is true; whatever he hears otherwise, the record cannot be as good unless our record agrees with it. 

Then he said, "Why do you write of those books burning, since it happened before you left? It is as if you were writing backward." 

"Do not worry about the method of my letters, *Mr. Pucci*," I said. I added, "I am told that unless you see my letters, you will not deliver them. You must excuse me for not letting you see them; I have told you enough of the content. If you will not deliver them, I can have them delivered in various ways, or I may choose not to send them at all and write a letter to the *Nuncio* stating that I had written an answer to his requests and the offer sent by *Fr. Pucci*, but that *Pucci* would not bring the letter unless he could see it himself." 

At length, after further discussion with *E. K.*, he resolved to go with the letter, and (by *E. K.'s* order) he was to receive 50 Dollars from <margin>Fifty Dollars.</margin> *John Carpio*, so that he would not be without money in *Prague*.

---

### N O T E.

<margin>Pucci's most manifest infidelity committed.</margin> This day, *Francis Pucci* said to us both, "How can you doubt my faithfulness toward you (whom I love as my own life), and against this Monster of *Rome*, whom it has long been my chief desire to see overthrown?" etc. Again, consider what faithfulness, obedience, and reverence he has promised to the *Pope* and this *Nuncio*, as specified in the writing he brought and so strongly urged us in many ways to accept.

Therefore *Fr.* is false to the *Pope*, or to us, or both; or he is rash, foolish, blind, etc. And (as our spiritual Schoolmaster several times calls him) "leprous." Therefore, I commit these actions of his to the judgment of God. But it is also greatly to be remembered and noted that he again discussed with *E. K.* the birth of *Christ*, saying it could not be proved by the Scriptures that *Christ* came from the line of *David* unless he were begotten through the actual sexual intercourse of *Joseph* with *Mary*. He said that because it was the gift of the Holy Spirit, *Christ* was conceived at *Joseph's* first and only carnal copulation with *Mary*; therefore she was considered (in a manner)

<margin>Namely, it is miraculous that a Virgin should conceive in her first encounter with a man.</margin>
...a Virgin according to the *Jews'* doctrine: when I heard this heresy, I trembled for the horror of such a manifest heresy against evident Scripture, *a virgin shall conceive and a virgin shall give birth*, etc., and against many other most plain and sufficient authorities both from the Scriptures and also histories of our Lady’s examination made by women, where she was found to be a Virgin, etc. And at her conception, her answer to the Angel: *Because I have not known a man*, etc., and *before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit*, etc.

### N O T E.

It is evident by this that this *Pucci* is very leprous, both in this heresy (and God knows what other heresies he is infected with) and also the previously proven infidelity.
On *Thursday*, July 17, *Fr. Pucci* began his journey toward *Prague* with my letter to the *Apostolic Nuncio*, and with letters to *John Carpio* from *E. K.*, and with my letters enclosed to the Lord *Rosenberg*. And we began our journey toward *Kassel*, but that night we rode only three miles, to *Gotha*; the horses we had hired were so poor that, sending them back again the next day, we hired a coach, etc.

## P O S T S C R I P T.

Remember that *Fr. Pucci*, the morning before his departure, asked me for a letter of recommendation to our friends regarding his loyalty toward us. "What is the need for that?" (I said), "for as much as your deeds were as well known to them as to us; your own conscience may serve you abundantly. But our various friends, who have warned us about you and have wondered why we would tolerate you any longer in our house and company, would not trust our letters yet in this case. They would also condemn us for poor judgment or great blindness in judging the case between you and us."
But truly I observed in him, now, a more proud presumption over us than before, when he was severely rebuked for acting superior to us, as he began to do.

<margin>Presumption.</margin>
1. Now he said he had as much authority as we do to publish any of our secrets at his discretion.
2. That he was entitled to eat bread with us.
3. That he understood our Books of Actions better than we did.
4. That he did not need our consent or advice to deal with the Pope's *Nuncio*: he did it by his general duty of charity, etc.
5. He offered to manage the *Nuncio* and the Emperor to reverse the decree made against us, etc.

### N O T E.

<margin>* See his writing concerning our Roman journey, etc.</margin>
Consider what this may imply: that the decree affected him as one of my household and one of those who then belonged to me, and whose name he is not afraid—in one way or another—to * thrust himself into the whole body of our revelations as a principal associate or receiver of them. By the first point, he ought to be afraid of the danger of the decree which banished us, unless he is assured of the goodwill of those who have shown themselves to be our mortal enemies; or else some other cause emboldened him for some other purpose, etc. By the second point, he might be afraid of such great presumption, being only a *Probationer*, not yet accepted, and known by us to be cut off.

<margin>J. D.</margin>
I cannot decipher and judge all these points, but refer them to the profound wisdom and high providence of God, as to why and how far He has allowed him to be privy to our Actions, and thus a sufficient witness for some purposes. May all things be to the honor and glory of God. *Amen*.

---

### Magnificent Lord,

Having read your letter, I was surprised to understand that you are of the opinion and belief that I have not a little hindered you and your associate in my duties with the Emperor, because I know myself to be so composed by both religion and nature that I desire to help everyone as much as possible and to hinder no one. However, that I have performed what was my duty ought not to be counted as a fault against me. Furthermore, since I am a mere intermediary between the Supreme Pontiff and the Emperor, I do not see what I can provide in this business of yours. However, I advise that you bring your innocence, your understanding of the Catholic faith, and the conversation and assistance of the Angels (which you say you have visibly) before the Supreme Pontiff and the Apostolic See, according to the decree of the Lateran Council in the eleventh session, and explain it so that it cannot be [doubtful] to anyone—

### $\Delta$ Divine Oracle.

Many are the lashes for those neglecting my commands: and manifold is the fury for men trusting in their own strength. For these despisers of my blood and of the strength of my Kingdom have become Giants in multiplying every abomination. But I am who I am, who placed the Throne in the Father and the Word to execute Judgment on the earth: who at the last Trumpet shall strike them, so that they are compelled to recognize my ways and return to their own fold. The iniquity of the Church and the people shall perish, and shall be judged by the sword. You indeed, William, extend your hand at the opportune time, as you shall be informed by me, and bring in the Kingdom (the most wicked one having been touched and dying): for I have anointed you in my strongest right hand to root out that false Prophet and Goliath <note>perhaps the Muslims and Turks</note> so that the Earth may understand the judgment from me, the crucified Nazarene. There are those who would sift you: but cursed are those plotting evil against you. Do good, and use my creatures for my glory. I have taught Kelley, restlessly, this night, concerning the other things which you shall learn from him. Let my spirit dwell in you.

-> At Trebona, at the end of August, 1589. <-

## Francesco Pucci prays for grace and peace from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ, to the most excellent and God-beloved men, Sir John Dee and Sir Edward Kelley, English gentlemen, elder brothers in Christ, and to be honored like fathers. Amen.

Since I left you, throughout that whole journey which I completed in eight days, having sold my horse at Leipzig, my spirit has been troubled quite a bit while I considered in my mind how many ways Satan has tried—and still does not cease to try—to delay the divine work and tear apart our union, using outward and inward schemes and weapons. For I can only recognize those inspirations of distrust, the rumors spread by envious men, the suspicions cast upon us without certain evidence against a faith proven by no small arguments, and obstacles and stumbling blocks of this kind, as coming from him. With these, that malignant spirit has set out to hinder our course and to pluck up and weaken the holy friendship begun between us under divine auspices.

Therefore, in that struggle, so that I might not give in to him in any way or grow weary, I have resolved to fortify myself more and more with a certain faith in God and hope in His promises, which I do not doubt He will keep. I also decided to persist more in frequent prayers to the Father Most High, that He might soon grant us that spirit by which our shoulders may become equal to "carrying mountains," as He says. To this end, I have decided to lead a more austere life and not to go to the lavish tables of friends, but to eat the bread of sorrow alone, *so that I may not be in a better condition than you, who are so greatly afflicted*, so that the most kind Lord may restore you to wholeness as soon as possible, and call us back together to our usual holy conversations and pious exercises, and gladden each of us with an outcome consistent with His most holy words.

The Lord gives me hope that by following this path, I may more easily prove my faith to you and others, and avoid many temptations that easily invade us among the men of this world. Therefore, unless driven by urgent necessity or common business, I flee all familiarity and social contact with courtiers, and in this way, I feel less unfit for prayers. I try daily to improve my life and character, so that I do not appear entirely unworthy of that school in which the Lord has deigned to teach me; nor meanwhile do I forget to pray, like that Publican, that God be merciful to me, a sinner. I do not doubt that you will help with your vows and supplications so that I may respond to my calling and be a help and consolation to you in the Lord's work. And that most kind Father will soon [turn] this adverse wind—

...he will see to it that his fire is more greatly kindled, and he will refresh us with greater joy than ever before. And so much for these matters. 

As for what concerns our business: I arrived here on the evening of July 24 and immediately went to the *Most Illustrious Lord Nuncio*, to whom I delivered your letters, which he seemed to receive with a joyful face. However, there was no time for conversation, as dinner was prepared and he wished to sit down. Being deferred until the following day, I went to *Lord Carpion*, only to learn that he had been sent to you and had departed from here four days earlier. I grieved greatly that I did not meet him, both on account of your letters and my own, since he was also carrying a certain packet for me. But what tormented me most was concern for the letters of the *Most Illustrious Lord Rosenburg*, which I knew were included in *Lord Carpion's* letters; I did not dare to open them or give them to another, since it was expressly written that the document was *for his own hands*. While I was seeking and waiting for an opportunity, one presented itself, which you shall soon hear. 

Returning the following day to the *Most Illustrious Lord Nuncio*, I found an *Italian Jesuit* with him, who had been my confessor. I was kindly received by both and ordered to sit; I was praised not a little by the *Jesuit* for my sincerity and integrity. Then I was gracefully advised by the *Most Illustrious Lord Nuncio* to assist him in converting that *Jesuit* (for he was the one who had complained to the Nuncio that he had granted me access too easily, arguing that *the testimonies of the Church triumphant are not subject to the judgment of the Church militant*). 

I replied that I had done what was in my power to teach him to prefer Heaven to earth and the higher tribunal to the lower; but since I had very little success, it was for the Nuncio, by his own doctrine and authority, to move the man from that opinion. The *Most Illustrious Lord Nuncio* readily approved our opinion in this matter and confirmed it with examples. He concluded by stating *that the certainty of one who sees and hears the Lord, or his angel, does not depend on Ecclesiastical proof, nor must he give an account of his revelation to the Church as long as he does not dare to exercise any public office. But if he begins to openly profess that he is taught and sent by God—so that it concerns not only himself but others to know by what spirit he is led—then it is the duty of Church officials to examine and prove his spirit. Nor can the person rightfully refuse this examination, even though he is not required to subject his revelations to them.* 

For if the ordinary authority has admitted him, all will be well, and no disturbances will be stirred up. But if through injury, ignorance, or some other such cause he is rejected, it will be his place to appeal to the Superior Lord who sent him, so that He may defend His servant and Legate, either by warning the ordinary Judge or by some other means. This he proved by a decree of the *Lateran Council*, which he mentions in his letters, and furthermore by the history of *St. Francis*, who was first expelled by *Pope Innocent* but was soon recalled after that ragged man appeared to the Pope in a dream, supporting the *Lateran* temple on his shoulders. He added, moreover, that the men of God are not accustomed to being deterred by one or two rejections, and this...

Regarding the manner of rejection, he was saying that Prelates sometimes used it to test the spirit and constancy of those who proposed new and great things. I, however, said that though these things may be so, *you have not until now attempted to exercise any public office, and have kept yourselves within private walls with the greatest modesty.* Then he, with a longer circuit of words, discussed you in such a way that he said it was now clear—from your own words—to the Most Serene King of Poland, the invincible Emperor, and the Most Illustrious Spanish Ambassador, that you are striving for something more than a private matter. And to the Supreme Pontiff, sitting in his watchtower over the entire Christian Republic, your persons could deservedly be suspect, searching as you do into the minds of Princes and the inner recesses of courts. This is also by reason of your Queen <note>Queen Elizabeth I</note>, who is most hostile to the Apostolic See and is conspiring with the Turk himself; and also because you have familiar spirits. Furthermore, it is because of your great skill in the hidden arts and sciences, by which the common people and the unlearned can easily be deceived. Since you are great <term>Astrologers</term>, he said, and it is easy for you to obtain the <term>geneses</term> <note>horoscopes or birth charts</note> of princes, and since you are skilled in the Magical arts, you could without difficulty propose things *in the name of good Angels* which actually stem from the spirit who is the enemy of the Church. 

Therefore, the Supreme Pontiff (for whom those two Princes are to be most carefully observed, seeing as they live and reign among Heretics) acted prudently in ordering that your morals and doctrine be investigated. However, it happened against his request and will *that you were expelled without your case being heard.* He said he truly grieves for your plight and is ready to see *that you are able to justify yourselves*; he asserted more than once that this was his desire. Therefore, he urged me to hasten to the *Most Illustrious Lord Rosenberg* and signify to him his good inclination toward you; for he will easily obtain from the Supreme Pontiff that your case be heard here. And if he favors you, as he has done so far, he [the Nuncio] would also be present to assist you with every service, and would be the first to throw himself at your knees *if you turn out to be such as some proclaim you to be.* 

I therefore went straight to the *Most Illustrious Lord Rosenberg.* But I had to return four times before I was admitted. On the 27th day, finally admitted, I set forth my devotion toward you and your affairs, and how the *Most Illustrious Lord Nuncio* was disposed toward you. Finally, I prayed that he would not desert that patronage and defense which he had undertaken of *the most pious strangers, who appealed from an Emperor ill-informed to an Emperor better-informed,* and who desired their innocence to be proven to God and men. He replied kindly: *That you were not very well known to him; that having spoken twice with the elder <note>John Dee</note> and only once with the younger <note>Edward Kelley</note>, he judged you learned, pious, and equipped with excellent gifts.* He thought that this had happened to you because of some bad report, a disadvantage to which the affairs of princes are subject; it was your part to bear it with an even mind. He said he did not repent that he had favored you, and if he knew what specifically you requested from him, he would labor to ensure your wishes were answered. Then it seemed to me I should say something about the excellent hope I had conceived of him...

I showed what a great stumbling block this would be to English *Catholics* and others, and what an opportunity would be given to heretics to attack the ecclesiastical order. I demonstrated that God has accustomed himself at other times to punish Catholic *Jews* through heretical Israelites; and finally, I declared how absurd it is for you to be condemned without your cause being heard, if you have deserved it; how much more absurd if you have not deserved any such thing; and most absurd indeed, since honor should rather be owed to you by the Catholic Church. On the 28th and 29th, I found the Illustrious Lord *Rosenberg* so busy that I could not be admitted, but through his chamberlain he indicated that he greatly desired for us to speak together, and so I should return on the 30th. In the meantime, I was again with the most Illustrious Lord Nuncio, who was soon to depart for the *Monastery of Saint Charles*, where he will stay as long as this heat rages.

And since it happened conveniently during our conversation, it seemed right to me to ask the man whether he approved of my opinion on how to discern, by certain signs and terms, the true word of God from the false and feigned, since an evil angel can transform himself into an angel of light, and false apostles often transfigure themselves into apostles of Christ. For I said two things seemed necessary to me for this judgment to be performed correctly: first, in the person listening, a good inclination and a heart well-disposed toward the Creator, depending entirely upon Him so that he holds nothing more important than pleasing Him, and who does not doubt His kindness and truth toward those who take refuge in Him to receive the good spirit. Second, that in the speech proposed in God's name, those properties are required which befit such an author, which *Paul* graphically describes when he says:

<margin>Hebrews 4:12, 13</margin>
*For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and there is no creature invisible in His sight.* To which God agrees, who says through *Jeremiah*:

<margin>Jeremiah 23:28, 29</margin>
*The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream, and he who has my words, let him tell my words. What has the straw to do with the wheat? says the Lord. Are not my words like fire? says the Lord, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?*

I concluded, therefore, that a person trusting in God detects the truth of the word of God from that efficacy and heat by which he feels himself affected. For the voice of the wolf and of the stranger shepherd cannot move the true sheep to follow him for long; and this is the rule by which I judged that divine pronouncements could be distinguished from the non-divine. He approved of my opinion, and added that without the good-will of the listeners, the efficacy of divine speeches does not appear, as is evident from the history of Christ. For while the simple *Israelites* were saying, "Has any man ever spoken like this?" and similar things about Christ's teaching, the *Pharisees* and perverse priests mocked and despised Him. Then I said, if it should happen then, that when we meet, the word of the Lord should come to you...

He replies that he also expects the man and wonders greatly at such a long delay, especially since Lord *Gregory*, who had gone to you with *Carpio* himself, had returned three days earlier. 

I, therefore, who knew nothing before of Lord *Gregory’s* journey or return, go straight to him. *Gallus*, his companion, admits me kindly, tells me to wait for the Doctor, and runs to fetch him. But since he delayed for some time, and I was just about to depart, I see Lord *Gregory* speaking privately with him and looking at me with a grim expression. I greet him and congratulate him on his return, and finally ask about you. 

He responds that he knows absolutely nothing of you or your affairs and has not been with you. Then I hesitate a little, and finally say that if he does not wish to say anything, I will bear it with a calm mind, but that it is already clear to me that he was with you. He is disgusted by your name and by the deceits and impostures of the whole world; he says his own affairs are his concern, not yours; that you promise many things but perform little, and he does not know why you complain. He says that for a year and a half, lured by vain hope, he stayed with you in order to learn some of your minor <term>arcanis</term> (secrets), yet he perceived nothing of any importance.
